source_records.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.JEL classificationD22; D82; M40; M41KeywordsCorporate disclosure; Industry information; Peer information; Organization of firms; Delegation of decision rights; Managerial learning; Within-firm agency frictionsIntroductionDelegation is essential for firm growth and improves aggregate productivity (Bloom et al., 2012, Akcigit et al., 2021). However, less is known about industry- or country-wide mechanisms that facilitate or impede the delegation of decision rights from the CEO to division managers (DMs). This paper focuses on one such mechanism: the peer information environment, i.e., the industry information generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them. Specifically, I study whether the peer information environment in the division’s industry and country affects the delegation of decision rights over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales from the CEO to DMs.I build on theoretical models of delegation (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Dessein, 2002, Harris and Raviv, 2005) to develop my prediction about how peer information can affect delegation. A basic framework in these models involves a CEO who considers delegating decision rights (e.g., over capital investment and hiring) to a DM because the DM has superior local information about factors such as customer needs and investment opportunities (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992). However, when the preferences of the CEO and DM are not fully aligned, delegation allows the DM to act on their own preferences rather than the CEO’s, creating agency frictions (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). Thus, delegation increases when (i) the DM has a greater information advantage over the CEO and (ii) the incentives of the CEO and DM are better aligned. Peer information affects both the DM’s information advantage and agency frictions of delegation.First, peer information can affect the DM’s information advantage over the CEO. Decisions made by firms in the same industry (e.g., capital investment, hiring) are influenced by similar economic forces, such as common shocks to profitability and investment opportunities (Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000). Thus, disclosures by peer firms and coverage by information intermediaries can provide information (e.g., earnings forecasts and investment plans) relevant to understanding these common industry factors, helping managers make more informed decisions. Since peer information is available to both the CEO and DMs, its effect on delegation depends on who learns more from it. On the one hand, if the CEO gains more new information, the DM’s information advantage narrows, reducing the benefit of relying on the DM’s knowledge, and thus reducing delegation (CEO learning channel). On the other hand, a richer peer information environment can increase delegation if the DM learns more. Garicano (2000) develops a theoretical model that relaxes the assumption that the DM has an information advantage and shows that delegation increases when more information becomes available, enabling DMs to acquire – at a lower cost – the knowledge needed to make informed decisions (DM learning channel).Second, peer information reduces agency frictions of delegation by helping the CEO better evaluate and monitor DMs (agency mitigation channel). For example, CEOs can use peer information to obtain relevant information about the costs of production, profitability, and investment expenditures in the industry, all of which provide useful benchmarks for filtering common shocks out of DMs’ performance and for monitoring DMs (Holmstrom, 1982, Nalebuff and Stiglitz, 1983, Cichello et al., 2009). Thus, the agency mitigation channel predicts that richer peer information reduces agency costs of delegation, motivating the CEO to increase delegation.To summarize, peer information can affect delegation through three channels. The agency mitigation and DM learning channels predict that a richer peer information environment increases delegation, whereas the CEO learning channel predicts the opposite. Thus, whether peer information increases or decreases delegation is ultimately an empirical question.Studying delegation within firms is challenging because it is largely unobservable to researchers (e.g., Prendergast, 2002). To overcome this challenge, I obtain information on the internal organization of firms using an international dataset from several waves of the World Management Survey (WMS) (Bloom et al., 2012, Scur et al., 2021). The WMS surveys a large number of randomly selected medium-sized public and private firms in North and South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. The WMS data are obtained through in-depth interviews with DMs using interview questions designed to be directly applicable to the theories of delegation discussed above (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). To measure the degree of delegation, I use the WMS data on DMs’ authority over four decisions: capital investment, hiring, investment in new products, and sales. The interviews are performed with one DM per firm. In addition to data on the degree of delegation, the WMS data include detailed information on the DM, division, and firm characteristics.To measure the richness of the peer information environment, I rely on prior research (Holmstrom, 1982, Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000, Shroff et al., 2017) and construct a proxy that captures (i) the relevance (i.e., informativeness) of peer information for understanding common industry factors and (ii) the aggregate amount of peer information available about these factors. To proxy for the relevance of peer information within an industry, I use the degree of earnings synchronicity in the industry. My intuition is that, when a peer firm’s earnings synchronicity is high, its earnings co-move more closely with industry-wide economic conditions, making its disclosures more informative about the common factors that also affect the focal firm’s division. I measure the aggregate amount of peer information using two proxies. The first proxy is the analyst coverage of peer firms in the industry (measured as the average number of analysts per peer firm). Prior research shows that analysts are industry experts who not only supply firm-specific and industry-level information through their reports (Brown et al., 2015), but also demand greater quantity and quality of disclosures from the firms they cover (Irani and Oesch, 2013, Christensen et al., 2021), thereby improving the peer information environment. My second proxy for the aggregate amount of peer information is the press coverage of peer firms. The press disseminates firm-initiated disclosures and produces new information through journalism (e.g., Bushee et al., 2010), enhancing the peer information environment. I calculate these three proxies by averaging across all firms in the division’s industry and country, excluding the focal firm. I then convert each proxy into a within-country quartile rank and average the three ranked proxies to construct my measure of the peer information environment.I test the relation between peer information and delegation using an international sample of 4908 unique public and private firms with 6663 firm-year observations over the 2005–2015 period. I find that firms with richer peer information delegate more, using a model that includes time-varying division-, firm-, and industry-level control variables that might affect delegation (e.g., firm size, incentive contracts, and internal information quality) as well as year×industry and year×country fixed effects. In terms of economic magnitude, an increase of one within-fixed effects standard deviation in peer information (resp. moving from the average firm in China to the average firm in the US) is associated with a 4% (resp. 13%) within-fixed effects standard deviation increase in delegation. These economic magnitudes are comparable to those reported by Bloom et al. (2012), who find that a one standard deviation increase in social trust is associated with a 7% standard deviation increase in delegation. My results are robust to alternative peer information measures and fixed effect structures.Next, I use three sets of tests to explore the potential channels underlying the relation between peer information and delegation: agency mitigation, CEO learning, and DM learning. First, I explore the agency mitigation channel. If peer information mitigates agency costs, its effect on delegation should be stronger when agency problems of delegation are greater. I explore two alternative mechanisms that mitigate agency problems: social trust and product market competition. When the CEO trusts the DM to act in the CEO’s interest, the agency frictions of delegation are lower. Consistent with this, Bloom et al. (2012) find that CEOs in high-trust regions delegate more. Similarly, DMs operating in competitive industries have stronger incentives to work hard and improve their performance because they have little slack (Bloom et al., 2010). Thus, these mechanisms reduce the need to monitor the DM. However, when these alternative mechanisms are weak, the importance of peer information for resolving agency frictions increases. Consistent with the agency mitigation channel, my results show that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when trust in the CEO’s region is lower and when competition in the DM’s industry is less intense.Second, I examine the CEO learning channel. The basic idea is that, if peer information affects delegation through CEO learning, its effect should vary with the CEO’s information set, e.g., a less informed CEO is more likely to learn from peer information. Although the CEO’s information set is not directly observable, I build on prior research and use proxies based on the CEO’s prior industry experience and tenure. Several studies document that greater industry experience and firm tenure lead to more informed decisions and reduce managers’ reliance on external information sources for learning (e.g., Cici et al., 2018, Guo and Zhong, 2023). These studies suggest that CEOs with less industry experience and shorter tenure are less informed and, therefore, more likely to learn from peer firms than those with extensive experience and longer tenure. Consistent with the CEO learning channel, which predicts that CEO learning reduces delegation, I find that the relation between peer information and delegation becomes negative when CEOs have less industry experience and when they have shorter tenure (i.e., when CEO learning is more likely).Third, I explore the DM learning channel using an idea similar to the one used for the CEO learning channel. If peer information impacts delegation by facilitating DM learning, its effect should depend on the DM’s information set, e.g., a less informed DM is more likely to learn from peer information. I use the DM’s tenure as a proxy for how informed the DM would be about the division and its industry absent peer information. A newly hired DM is less likely to possess extensive knowledge about the division’s operations. As DMs’ tenure increases, they acquire a deeper understanding of the division’s operations, industry dynamics, and how these industry-level factors impact the division. Thus, a DM with shorter tenure is more likely to learn from peer information. Consistent with the DM learning channel, which predicts that DM learning motivates the CEO to delegate more, I find that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when DMs have shorter tenure.Examining the peer information environment rather than the firm’s own can mitigate concerns that the firm endogenously determines both delegation and its information environment. However, the peer effects literature faces its own empirical challenges (Manski, 1993; Section 4.6.2 Angrist and Pischke, 2009). A standard concern in this literature is that common characteristics or shocks may drive both peers’ and the focal firm’s outcomes, leading to omitted variable bias. For instance, consider an industry-wide shock to investment opportunities (e.g., a technological innovation). Firms in the industry, both the focal firm and its peers, may respond by (i) investing and growing larger, which can motivate greater delegation, and (ii) raising external capital to fund these investments, which can motivate greater disclosure to facilitate this financing. Thus, the common shock can increase both the focal firm’s delegation and peer disclosure, generating a positive association between the two even in the absence of any causal effect.I take several steps to mitigate such endogeneity concerns. First, I find that the results are robust to including a battery of control variables as well as year×industry, year×country, and industry×country fixed effects. Second, using the test developed by Oster (2019), I find that, to move the estimated effect to zero, omitted variables would need to be 5.69 times as important as my control variables, which seems unlikely. Third, and more importantly, I employ an alternative identification strategy using a simulated instrument that exploits threshold-induced variation in the extent of financial reporting requirements across industries in Europe (Breuer, 2021, Breuer, 2025). Using this instrument, I find that mandating a greater share of firms in an industry to disclose their financial statements increases delegation within firms in that industry.This paper makes several contributions. My study relates to the empirical literature on the factors influencing the internal allocation of decision rights. This literature links delegation to social trust (Bloom et al., 2012); personal characteristics of the CEO and characteristics of the decision (Graham et al., 2015); a firm’s own organizational design, information technology, and predictive analytics (e.g., Baiman et al., 1995, Abernethy et al., 2004, Indjejikian and Matejka, 2012, Bloom et al., 2014, Labro et al., 2023); and the firm’s operating environment (e.g., Acemoglu et al., 2007, Campbell et al., 2009, Bloom et al., 2010, Robinson and Stocken, 2013).1 My study contributes to this literature in two ways: (i) I propose external financial reporting and disclosure as a mechanism that facilitates delegation; and (ii) I extend the prior research exploring mechanisms that reduce agency frictions of delegation within firms, including incentive contracts in Abernethy et al. (2004) and social trust in Bloom et al. (2012), by documenting that a richer information environment reduces these frictions.In addition, this paper relates to the literature examining the real effects of financial reporting and disclosure, particularly on investment decisions.2 My study extends this literature in two ways. First, in their review of the real effects literature, Roychowdhury et al. (2019) note, “Overall, it appears that most of the literature has concentrated on classic agency frictions arising from manager-shareholder conflicts, whereas other agency conflicts have received less attention” [emphasis added]. I extend the literature by documenting that peer information increases delegation by reducing agency conflicts within firms between the CEO and DMs. Shroff et al. (2014) also explore agency frictions between the parent and subsidiaries within multinational companies by examining capital investment efficiency. I complement their study by exploring the effects of peer information on delegation within firms. Second, Labro and Pierk (2026) highlight that most studies in this literature document the effects of financial reporting on corporate decisions (e.g., capital investment) but provide limited direct evidence on the management (accounting) practices that support those decisions, likely because such practices are generally unobservable to researchers. My study answers their call for more direct evidence by examining one such management practice: the delegation of decision rights within firms, which can lead to more informed decisions (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992).Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsPeer information environment and delegationTheoretical work exploring the delegation of decision rights from the principal (CEO in my setting) to the agent (DM in my setting) highlights (i) the efficiency of using the local information dispersed among individuals and (ii) the agency frictions of delegating decision rights (e.g., Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992, Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Harris and Raviv, 2005). fields.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

before.title_zh: 企业内部的管理层授权与同行信息环境
before.abstract_zh: 本文考察同行信息环境——由同行企业的披露以及覆盖这些企业的信息中介所产生——是否以及如何影响CEO将决策权授予部门经理（DM）。利用一个国际调查数据集，我衡量了企业在资本投资、人力资本投资、新产品投资和销售方面决策的內部授权程度。我发现，在同行信息环境更丰富的国家-行业中，CEO会向部门经理授予更多权力。横截面检验凸显了三个潜在渠道。具体而言，结果表明，同行信息（i）帮助CEO获取信息，以减少相对于DM的潜在信息劣势（CEO学习），（ii）缓解CEO-DM代理摩擦（代理缓解），以及（iii）为DM提供相关信息以做出更好的决策（DM学习）。虽然CEO学习会减少授权，但代理缓解和DM学习会增加授权。这些发现提供了证据，表明关于同行的信息会影响企业的内部组织。

I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.JEL classificationD22; D82; M40; M41KeywordsCorporate disclosure; Industry information; Peer information; Organization of firms; Delegation of decision rights; Managerial learning; Within-firm agency frictionsIntroductionDelegation is essential for firm growth and improves aggregate productivity (Bloom et al., 2012, Akcigit et al., 2021). However, less is known about industry- or country-wide mechanisms that facilitate or impede the delegation of decision rights from the CEO to division managers (DMs). This paper focuses on one such mechanism: the peer information environment, i.e., the industry information generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them. Specifically, I study whether the peer information environment in the division’s industry and country affects the delegation of decision rights over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales from the CEO to DMs.I build on theoretical models of delegation (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Dessein, 2002, Harris and Raviv, 2005) to develop my prediction about how peer information can affect delegation. A basic framework in these models involves a CEO who considers delegating decision rights (e.g., over capital investment and hiring) to a DM because the DM has superior local information about factors such as customer needs and investment opportunities (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992). However, when the preferences of the CEO and DM are not fully aligned, delegation allows the DM to act on their own preferences rather than the CEO’s, creating agency frictions (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). Thus, delegation increases when (i) the DM has a greater information advantage over the CEO and (ii) the incentives of the CEO and DM are better aligned. Peer information affects both the DM’s information advantage and agency frictions of delegation.First, peer information can affect the DM’s information advantage over the CEO. Decisions made by firms in the same industry (e.g., capital investment, hiring) are influenced by similar economic forces, such as common shocks to profitability and investment opportunities (Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000). Thus, disclosures by peer firms and coverage by information intermediaries can provide information (e.g., earnings forecasts and investment plans) relevant to understanding these common industry factors, helping managers make more informed decisions. Since peer information is available to both the CEO and DMs, its effect on delegation depends on who learns more from it. On the one hand, if the CEO gains more new information, the DM’s information advantage narrows, reducing the benefit of relying on the DM’s knowledge, and thus reducing delegation (CEO learning channel). On the other hand, a richer peer information environment can increase delegation if the DM learns more. Garicano (2000) develops a theoretical model that relaxes the assumption that the DM has an information advantage and shows that delegation increases when more information becomes available, enabling DMs to acquire – at a lower cost – the knowledge needed to make informed decisions (DM learning channel).Second, peer information reduces agency frictions of delegation by helping the CEO better evaluate and monitor DMs (agency mitigation channel). For example, CEOs can use peer information to obtain relevant information about the costs of production, profitability, and investment expenditures in the industry, all of which provide useful benchmarks for filtering common shocks out of DMs’ performance and for monitoring DMs (Holmstrom, 1982, Nalebuff and Stiglitz, 1983, Cichello et al., 2009). Thus, the agency mitigation channel predicts that richer peer information reduces agency costs of delegation, motivating the CEO to increase delegation.To summarize, peer information can affect delegation through three channels. The agency mitigation and DM learning channels predict that a richer peer information environment increases delegation, whereas the CEO learning channel predicts the opposite. Thus, whether peer information increases or decreases delegation is ultimately an empirical question.Studying delegation within firms is challenging because it is largely unobservable to researchers (e.g., Prendergast, 2002). To overcome this challenge, I obtain information on the internal organization of firms using an international dataset from several waves of the World Management Survey (WMS) (Bloom et al., 2012, Scur et al., 2021). The WMS surveys a large number of randomly selected medium-sized public and private firms in North and South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. The WMS data are obtained through in-depth interviews with DMs using interview questions designed to be directly applicable to the theories of delegation discussed above (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). To measure the degree of delegation, I use the WMS data on DMs’ authority over four decisions: capital investment, hiring, investment in new products, and sales. The interviews are performed with one DM per firm. In addition to data on the degree of delegation, the WMS data include detailed information on the DM, division, and firm characteristics.To measure the richness of the peer information environment, I rely on prior research (Holmstrom, 1982, Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000, Shroff et al., 2017) and construct a proxy that captures (i) the relevance (i.e., informativeness) of peer information for understanding common industry factors and (ii) the aggregate amount of peer information available about these factors. To proxy for the relevance of peer information within an industry, I use the degree of earnings synchronicity in the industry. My intuition is that, when a peer firm’s earnings synchronicity is high, its earnings co-move more closely with industry-wide economic conditions, making its disclosures more informative about the common factors that also affect the focal firm’s division. I measure the aggregate amount of peer information using two proxies. The first proxy is the analyst coverage of peer firms in the industry (measured as the average number of analysts per peer firm). Prior research shows that analysts are industry experts who not only supply firm-specific and industry-level information through their reports (Brown et al., 2015), but also demand greater quantity and quality of disclosures from the firms they cover (Irani and Oesch, 2013, Christensen et al., 2021), thereby improving the peer information environment. My second proxy for the aggregate amount of peer information is the press coverage of peer firms. The press disseminates firm-initiated disclosures and produces new information through journalism (e.g., Bushee et al., 2010), enhancing the peer information environment. I calculate these three proxies by averaging across all firms in the division’s industry and country, excluding the focal firm. I then convert each proxy into a within-country quartile rank and average the three ranked proxies to construct my measure of the peer information environment.I test the relation between peer information and delegation using an international sample of 4908 unique public and private firms with 6663 firm-year observations over the 2005–2015 period. I find that firms with richer peer information delegate more, using a model that includes time-varying division-, firm-, and industry-level control variables that might affect delegation (e.g., firm size, incentive contracts, and internal information quality) as well as year×industry and year×country fixed effects. In terms of economic magnitude, an increase of one within-fixed effects standard deviation in peer information (resp. moving from the average firm in China to the average firm in the US) is associated with a 4% (resp. 13%) within-fixed effects standard deviation increase in delegation. These economic magnitudes are comparable to those reported by Bloom et al. (2012), who find that a one standard deviation increase in social trust is associated with a 7% standard deviation increase in delegation. My results are robust to alternative peer information measures and fixed effect structures.Next, I use three sets of tests to explore the potential channels underlying the relation between peer information and delegation: agency mitigation, CEO learning, and DM learning. First, I explore the agency mitigation channel. If peer information mitigates agency costs, its effect on delegation should be stronger when agency problems of delegation are greater. I explore two alternative mechanisms that mitigate agency problems: social trust and product market competition. When the CEO trusts the DM to act in the CEO’s interest, the agency frictions of delegation are lower. Consistent with this, Bloom et al. (2012) find that CEOs in high-trust regions delegate more. Similarly, DMs operating in competitive industries have stronger incentives to work hard and improve their performance because they have little slack (Bloom et al., 2010). Thus, these mechanisms reduce the need to monitor the DM. However, when these alternative mechanisms are weak, the importance of peer information for resolving agency frictions increases. Consistent with the agency mitigation channel, my results show that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when trust in the CEO’s region is lower and when competition in the DM’s industry is less intense.Second, I examine the CEO learning channel. The basic idea is that, if peer information affects delegation through CEO learning, its effect should vary with the CEO’s information set, e.g., a less informed CEO is more likely to learn from peer information. Although the CEO’s information set is not directly observable, I build on prior research and use proxies based on the CEO’s prior industry experience and tenure. Several studies document that greater industry experience and firm tenure lead to more informed decisions and reduce managers’ reliance on external information sources for learning (e.g., Cici et al., 2018, Guo and Zhong, 2023). These studies suggest that CEOs with less industry experience and shorter tenure are less informed and, therefore, more likely to learn from peer firms than those with extensive experience and longer tenure. Consistent with the CEO learning channel, which predicts that CEO learning reduces delegation, I find that the relation between peer information and delegation becomes negative when CEOs have less industry experience and when they have shorter tenure (i.e., when CEO learning is more likely).Third, I explore the DM learning channel using an idea similar to the one used for the CEO learning channel. If peer information impacts delegation by facilitating DM learning, its effect should depend on the DM’s information set, e.g., a less informed DM is more likely to learn from peer information. I use the DM’s tenure as a proxy for how informed the DM would be about the division and its industry absent peer information. A newly hired DM is less likely to possess extensive knowledge about the division’s operations. As DMs’ tenure increases, they acquire a deeper understanding of the division’s operations, industry dynamics, and how these industry-level factors impact the division. Thus, a DM with shorter tenure is more likely to learn from peer information. Consistent with the DM learning channel, which predicts that DM learning motivates the CEO to delegate more, I find that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when DMs have shorter tenure.Examining the peer information environment rather than the firm’s own can mitigate concerns that the firm endogenously determines both delegation and its information environment. However, the peer effects literature faces its own empirical challenges (Manski, 1993; Section 4.6.2 Angrist and Pischke, 2009). A standard concern in this literature is that common characteristics or shocks may drive both peers’ and the focal firm’s outcomes, leading to omitted variable bias. For instance, consider an industry-wide shock to investment opportunities (e.g., a technological innovation). Firms in the industry, both the focal firm and its peers, may respond by (i) investing and growing larger, which can motivate greater delegation, and (ii) raising external capital to fund these investments, which can motivate greater disclosure to facilitate this financing. Thus, the common shock can increase both the focal firm’s delegation and peer disclosure, generating a positive association between the two even in the absence of any causal effect.I take several steps to mitigate such endogeneity concerns. First, I find that the results are robust to including a battery of control variables as well as year×industry, year×country, and industry×country fixed effects. Second, using the test developed by Oster (2019), I find that, to move the estimated effect to zero, omitted variables would need to be 5.69 times as important as my control variables, which seems unlikely. Third, and more importantly, I employ an alternative identification strategy using a simulated instrument that exploits threshold-induced variation in the extent of financial reporting requirements across industries in Europe (Breuer, 2021, Breuer, 2025). Using this instrument, I find that mandating a greater share of firms in an industry to disclose their financial statements increases delegation within firms in that industry.This paper makes several contributions. My study relates to the empirical literature on the factors influencing the internal allocation of decision rights. This literature links delegation to social trust (Bloom et al., 2012); personal characteristics of the CEO and characteristics of the decision (Graham et al., 2015); a firm’s own organizational design, information technology, and predictive analytics (e.g., Baiman et al., 1995, Abernethy et al., 2004, Indjejikian and Matejka, 2012, Bloom et al., 2014, Labro et al., 2023); and the firm’s operating environment (e.g., Acemoglu et al., 2007, Campbell et al., 2009, Bloom et al., 2010, Robinson and Stocken, 2013).1 My study contributes to this literature in two ways: (i) I propose external financial reporting and disclosure as a mechanism that facilitates delegation; and (ii) I extend the prior research exploring mechanisms that reduce agency frictions of delegation within firms, including incentive contracts in Abernethy et al. (2004) and social trust in Bloom et al. (2012), by documenting that a richer information environment reduces these frictions.In addition, this paper relates to the literature examining the real effects of financial reporting and disclosure, particularly on investment decisions.2 My study extends this literature in two ways. First, in their review of the real effects literature, Roychowdhury et al. (2019) note, “Overall, it appears that most of the literature has concentrated on classic agency frictions arising from manager-shareholder conflicts, whereas other agency conflicts have received less attention” [emphasis added]. I extend the literature by documenting that peer information increases delegation by reducing agency conflicts within firms between the CEO and DMs. Shroff et al. (2014) also explore agency frictions between the parent and subsidiaries within multinational companies by examining capital investment efficiency. I complement their study by exploring the effects of peer information on delegation within firms. Second, Labro and Pierk (2026) highlight that most studies in this literature document the effects of financial reporting on corporate decisions (e.g., capital investment) but provide limited direct evidence on the management (accounting) practices that support those decisions, likely because such practices are generally unobservable to researchers. My study answers their call for more direct evidence by examining one such management practice: the delegation of decision rights within firms, which can lead to more informed decisions (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992).Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsPeer information environment and delegationTheoretical work exploring the delegation of decision rights from the principal (CEO in my setting) to the agent (DM in my setting) highlights (i) the efficiency of using the local information dispersed among individuals and (ii) the agency frictions of delegating decision rights (e.g., Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992, Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Harris and Raviv, 2005). proposed.title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
proposed.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

after.title_zh: 企业内部的管理层授权与同行信息环境
after.abstract_zh: 本文考察同行信息环境——由同行企业的披露以及覆盖这些企业的信息中介所产生——是否以及如何影响CEO将决策权授予部门经理（DM）。利用一个国际调查数据集，我衡量了企业在资本投资、人力资本投资、新产品投资和销售方面决策的內部授权程度。我发现，在同行信息环境更丰富的国家-行业中，CEO会向部门经理授予更多权力。横截面检验凸显了三个潜在渠道。具体而言，结果表明，同行信息（i）帮助CEO获取信息，以减少相对于DM的潜在信息劣势（CEO学习），（ii）缓解CEO-DM代理摩擦（代理缓解），以及（iii）为DM提供相关信息以做出更好的决策（DM学习）。虽然CEO学习会减少授权，但代理缓解和DM学习会增加授权。这些发现提供了证据，表明关于同行的信息会影响企业的内部组织。

source_records.title: Direct and Indirect Effects of Transparency Regulation
source_records.abstract: We examine the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation on economic activity. Using two distinct sources of regulatory variation—the varying extent of financial-reporting requirements and the staggered introduction of electronic business registers in Europe—, we find that direct exposure to transparency regulation tends to hurt focal firms’ economic activity (e.g., production and employment). By contrast, we find that indirect exposure to transparency regulation imposed on other related firms tends to help focal firms’ economic activity. In terms of relative magnitudes, we find that the negative direct and positive indirect effects tend to be of similar size, almost perfectly offsetting each other. Collectively, our evidence suggests that transparency regulation appears to primarily reallocate economic activity from more toward less regulated markets rather than help or hurt aggregate economic activity.

before.title_zh: 透明度监管的直接效应与间接效应
before.abstract_zh: 我们考察透明度监管对经济活动的直接效应与间接效应。利用两种不同的监管变异来源——财务报告要求的程度差异以及欧洲电子企业登记册的分阶段引入——，我们发现，直接暴露于透明度监管往往会损害焦点企业的经济活动（例如生产和就业）。相比之下，我们发现，由施加于其他关联企业的透明度监管所带来的间接暴露，往往有助于焦点企业的经济活动。就相对幅度而言，我们发现负向直接效应与正向间接效应往往规模相近，几乎完全相互抵消。总体而言，我们的证据表明，透明度监管似乎主要是将经济活动从监管较多的市场重新配置到监管较少的市场，而非帮助或损害总体经济活动。

By contrast, we find that indirect exposure to transparency regulation imposed on other related firms tends to help focal firms’ economic activity. In terms of relative magnitudes, we find that the negative direct and positive indirect effects tend to be of similar size, almost perfectly offsetting each other. Collectively, our evidence suggests that transparency regulation appears to primarily reallocate economic activity from more toward less regulated markets rather than help or hurt aggregate economic activity.

after.title_zh: 透明度监管的直接效应与间接效应
after.abstract_zh: 我们考察透明度监管对经济活动的直接效应与间接效应。利用两种不同的监管变异来源——财务报告要求的程度差异以及欧洲电子企业登记册的分阶段引入——，我们发现，直接暴露于透明度监管往往会损害焦点企业的经济活动（例如生产和就业）。相比之下，我们发现，由施加于其他关联企业的透明度监管所带来的间接暴露，往往有助于焦点企业的经济活动。就相对幅度而言，我们发现负向直接效应与正向间接效应往往规模相近，几乎完全相互抵消。总体而言，我们的证据表明，透明度监管似乎主要是将经济活动从监管较多的市场重新配置到监管较少的市场，而非帮助或损害总体经济活动。

source_records.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
source_records.abstract: I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.KeywordsAccounting standards; Financial reporting quality; Audit quality; Resource constraintsJEL classificationM41; M42; M49IntroductionSince the Accounting Standard Codification (ASC) project launched in 2009, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) has issued more than 200 accounting standards updates (ASUs). Most new standards include a section titled “Benefits and Costs,” where the FASB justifies the potential increased cost of financial statement preparation with the additional benefit of improved information quality. Prior research has provided insights about the effects of specific, prominent standards (e.g., Henry et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2019; Tillet, 2026), but there is a paucity of evidence about whether and to what extent FASB standards satisfy the FASB's intent noted in each standard. As prominent standards examined in other studies often involve sweeping changes and are not representative of typical standards, our understanding of the influence of new standards on financial reporting quality is limited. Recent research indicates that firms have limited accounting expertise (Huang et al., 2025) and their behavior toward the typical standard differs from their preparation for prominent standards (e.g., revenue), which suggests that firms may not have available resources to implement new standards. In this study, I examine how new accounting standards affect financial reporting quality and which factors moderate this relationship.Despite more than 15 standards, on average, becoming effective each year, prior studies provide few details about the challenges firms and their auditors face during implementation. Yet, adopting new standards has the potential to affect financial reporting quality for several reasons. Firms often must re-evaluate their existing procedures, implement new IT systems, or hire additional personnel. In addition, adoption increases the workload for both preparers and their auditors, and both groups’ performance declines under such conditions (Chen et al., 2023; Christensen et al., 2021a). Given the ongoing accounting resource strains (AICPA, 2023) and the difficulty investors face when standards change (Dyer et al., 2025), it is important to understand how the implementation of standards influences financial reporting quality.To conduct my empirical analyses, I must identify which firms are affected by new accounting standards. This task is challenging due to varying language and disclosure choices among adopting firms. Prior studies have addressed this challenge by focusing on a single, prominent standard that produced an observable financial statement effect (e.g., Hunsader et al., 2022) or by identifying the types of firms likely affected by a single, new standard (e.g., Khan et al., 2018). As my analysis investigates the effects across all new standards, I develop a new method to identify affected firms. That is, I use a novel AI-based tool to parse more than 50,000 XBRL disclosures and identify firms adopting any standard that materially affects their financial statements. I then examine how standards adoption affects firms’ financial reporting quality.I find that adoption occurs frequently and that it negatively influences the quality of financial reporting. Approximately 37 percent of firm years across my sample are involved in the adoption of a new standard that has a material impact. Moreover, I find that adopting firms are 31 percent more likely to restate their annual filings through an item 4.02 disclosure (Big R restatements) and 44 percent more likely to fail to disclose an existing material weakness than firms unaffected by a new standard. Thus, new standards appear to have an immediate, detrimental effect on financial reporting quality.To better understand how standards adoption harms financial reporting quality, I examine two potential drivers of this effect. First, the firm may face challenges in implementing the standard's requirements, resulting in improper reporting about the subject matter of the standard. With a new standard, firms may not have pertinent expertise or resources to implement the standard without error. Alternatively, firms and their auditors likely recognize the possibility of increased regulatory scrutiny of areas affected by the standard, so they may devote sufficient effort to ensure those areas are reported properly. However, this increased attention may draw resources away from other financial reporting areas, resulting in lower financial reporting quality in areas unaffected by new standards (Kahneman, 1973; Seidel, 2017).To test these competing explanations, I examine the restatement categories associated with standards adoption. I find that the detrimental effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated in accounting areas unrelated to the new standard and completed late in the audit. I corroborate these findings with SEC comment letters. I find that firms adopting new standards are 6.5 percent more likely to receive an SEC comment letter, but I fail to find evidence that these comment letters reference the new standards. Results from these tests suggest that standards adoption diverts firm and auditor attention to the new standard and away from other areas. To corroborate this inference, I examine the duration of this effect. If the impairment stems from a diversion of firm and auditor resources during the adoption, the effect will likely dissipate after the adoption is completed. I find that the reduction in financial reporting quality is evident only in the year of adoption. Collectively, the evidence suggests that the adoption of a new accounting standard is associated with a decrease in financial reporting quality that is concentrated in the adoption year in areas unrelated to the standard itself.I expect that the effect on financial reporting quality differs based on firm, standard, and auditor characteristics, so I next test how these factors influence its magnitude. Regarding firm-level factors, recent research (Huang et al., 2025) suggests that firms often lack sufficient internal accounting expertise to handle increases in workloads that may be required to adopt a standard. I find that financial reporting quality impairments are more pronounced when firms are in unregulated industries, have ongoing mergers, experience accounting personnel turnover, or have existing internal control deficiencies. Collectively, this evidence suggests that concurrent accounting-related challenges influence the effect of adopting new accounting standards.Second, I investigate standard-level factors that may influence the success of adoption. Accounting standards vary in their scope, with some simply modifying minor disclosure requirements while others require significant accounting policy changes. More complex standards are more likely to require additional work from firms and their auditors, which may lead to lower financial reporting quality. I use three proxies for standards complexity: the FOG index, the length of the standard, and the degree to which auditors lobbied for the standard.1 I find that the complexity of the adopted standard exacerbates new standards’ impairment of financial reporting quality.Third, I consider whether auditor-related factors affect the success of the adoption of standards. Auditors can provide assistance to their clients only insofar as they have available resources to increase staffing. Because standards implementation requires additional work, auditors generally attempt to allocate additional employees to affected clients. However, their ability to do so depends on the availability of additional auditors. I expect that offices with more clients concurrently adopting new standards will have fewer available personnel and be less successful in helping clients adopt the latest standards. Consistent with this expectation, I find that the negative effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated among offices that have more clients adopting new standards. I also find that the results are more pronounced for clients of non-Big 4 auditors, which is consistent with Big 4 auditors having more training and support resources, enabling more efficient audit program modifications.Finally, I conduct semi-structured interviews with financial statement preparers and audit partners to provide additional institutional context about how firms and their auditors collaborate to implement new standards.2 Interviewees note that the implementation of new standards requires significant effort and disrupts other processes and that firms often turn to their auditors for implementation guidance. Overall, the interviewees provide insights consistent with my empirical analyses.This study makes several contributions to the literature. While prior studies indicate certain prominent standards achieve targeted regulatory objectives, like improving inter-industry revenue comparability (Tillet, 2026), I find that the adoption of standards in general is associated with lower financial reporting quality. Importantly, the evidence suggests that new standards create a distraction effect that lowers financial reporting quality in areas unrelated to the standard being adopted. I also find that client, standard, and auditor-related factors influence the success of implementation. The FASB regularly conducts post-implementation reviews to examine unintended consequences or costs of standards, and these findings provide relevant feedback on the adoption process. This study suggests that one unintended consequence of a new standard is a negative effect on financial reporting quality in the year of adoption.Second, this study introduces a novel AI-based methodology to parse annual reports. Recent research across several streams of literature relies on various methodologies to glean insights from unstructured textual disclosures ranging from basic keyword searches to deep learning neural networks (see Bochkay et al., 2023 for a recent review). While some studies have begun using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) for identification (Bernard et al., 2026), this is the first study using a standard, publicly available LLM model for identification. proposed.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
proposed.abstract:
•
Accounting standards adoption leads to lower financial reporting quality.
•
Adopting firms are 31% more likely to misstate financial statements.
•
The misstatements are observable only in the year of adoption.
•
The misstatements involve areas unrelated to the new accounting standards.
•
Results are more pronounced in resource-constrained firms and auditors.

existing_records.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
existing_records.abstract: I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

before.title_zh: 应对新会计准则：对企业及其审计师的影响
before.abstract_zh: 我考察了实施新会计准则对财务报告质量的影响。尽管先前研究表明准则总体上实现了其监管目标，但近期文献发现企业面临显著的技术会计能力约束，这促使我们需要探究会计准则采用对财务报告质量更广泛的影响。我采用一种新颖的基于人工智能的方法来识别受新会计准则影响的企业，发现当企业实施新准则时，财务报告质量下降。证据表明，受损的财务报告质量出现在与新准则无关的会计领域，这与分心效应一致。当企业同时面临其他与会计相关的挑战、会计准则更为复杂以及审计师资源受限时，结果更为显著。这些发现为新会计准则的意外后果提供了证据，并为缓解这些成本的潜在途径提供了启示。

While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.KeywordsAccounting standards; Financial reporting quality; Audit quality; Resource constraintsJEL classificationM41; M42; M49IntroductionSince the Accounting Standard Codification (ASC) project launched in 2009, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) has issued more than 200 accounting standards updates (ASUs). Most new standards include a section titled “Benefits and Costs,” where the FASB justifies the potential increased cost of financial statement preparation with the additional benefit of improved information quality. Prior research has provided insights about the effects of specific, prominent standards (e.g., Henry et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2019; Tillet, 2026), but there is a paucity of evidence about whether and to what extent FASB standards satisfy the FASB's intent noted in each standard. As prominent standards examined in other studies often involve sweeping changes and are not representative of typical standards, our understanding of the influence of new standards on financial reporting quality is limited. Recent research indicates that firms have limited accounting expertise (Huang et al., 2025) and their behavior toward the typical standard differs from their preparation for prominent standards (e.g., revenue), which suggests that firms may not have available resources to implement new standards. In this study, I examine how new accounting standards affect financial reporting quality and which factors moderate this relationship.Despite more than 15 standards, on average, becoming effective each year, prior studies provide few details about the challenges firms and their auditors face during implementation. Yet, adopting new standards has the potential to affect financial reporting quality for several reasons. Firms often must re-evaluate their existing procedures, implement new IT systems, or hire additional personnel. In addition, adoption increases the workload for both preparers and their auditors, and both groups’ performance declines under such conditions (Chen et al., 2023; Christensen et al., 2021a). Given the ongoing accounting resource strains (AICPA, 2023) and the difficulty investors face when standards change (Dyer et al., 2025), it is important to understand how the implementation of standards influences financial reporting quality.To conduct my empirical analyses, I must identify which firms are affected by new accounting standards. This task is challenging due to varying language and disclosure choices among adopting firms. Prior studies have addressed this challenge by focusing on a single, prominent standard that produced an observable financial statement effect (e.g., Hunsader et al., 2022) or by identifying the types of firms likely affected by a single, new standard (e.g., Khan et al., 2018). As my analysis investigates the effects across all new standards, I develop a new method to identify affected firms. That is, I use a novel AI-based tool to parse more than 50,000 XBRL disclosures and identify firms adopting any standard that materially affects their financial statements. I then examine how standards adoption affects firms’ financial reporting quality.I find that adoption occurs frequently and that it negatively influences the quality of financial reporting. Approximately 37 percent of firm years across my sample are involved in the adoption of a new standard that has a material impact. Moreover, I find that adopting firms are 31 percent more likely to restate their annual filings through an item 4.02 disclosure (Big R restatements) and 44 percent more likely to fail to disclose an existing material weakness than firms unaffected by a new standard. Thus, new standards appear to have an immediate, detrimental effect on financial reporting quality.To better understand how standards adoption harms financial reporting quality, I examine two potential drivers of this effect. First, the firm may face challenges in implementing the standard's requirements, resulting in improper reporting about the subject matter of the standard. With a new standard, firms may not have pertinent expertise or resources to implement the standard without error. Alternatively, firms and their auditors likely recognize the possibility of increased regulatory scrutiny of areas affected by the standard, so they may devote sufficient effort to ensure those areas are reported properly. However, this increased attention may draw resources away from other financial reporting areas, resulting in lower financial reporting quality in areas unaffected by new standards (Kahneman, 1973; Seidel, 2017).To test these competing explanations, I examine the restatement categories associated with standards adoption. I find that the detrimental effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated in accounting areas unrelated to the new standard and completed late in the audit. I corroborate these findings with SEC comment letters. I find that firms adopting new standards are 6.5 percent more likely to receive an SEC comment letter, but I fail to find evidence that these comment letters reference the new standards. Results from these tests suggest that standards adoption diverts firm and auditor attention to the new standard and away from other areas. To corroborate this inference, I examine the duration of this effect. If the impairment stems from a diversion of firm and auditor resources during the adoption, the effect will likely dissipate after the adoption is completed. I find that the reduction in financial reporting quality is evident only in the year of adoption. Collectively, the evidence suggests that the adoption of a new accounting standard is associated with a decrease in financial reporting quality that is concentrated in the adoption year in areas unrelated to the standard itself.I expect that the effect on financial reporting quality differs based on firm, standard, and auditor characteristics, so I next test how these factors influence its magnitude. Regarding firm-level factors, recent research (Huang et al., 2025) suggests that firms often lack sufficient internal accounting expertise to handle increases in workloads that may be required to adopt a standard. I find that financial reporting quality impairments are more pronounced when firms are in unregulated industries, have ongoing mergers, experience accounting personnel turnover, or have existing internal control deficiencies. Collectively, this evidence suggests that concurrent accounting-related challenges influence the effect of adopting new accounting standards.Second, I investigate standard-level factors that may influence the success of adoption. Accounting standards vary in their scope, with some simply modifying minor disclosure requirements while others require significant accounting policy changes. More complex standards are more likely to require additional work from firms and their auditors, which may lead to lower financial reporting quality. I use three proxies for standards complexity: the FOG index, the length of the standard, and the degree to which auditors lobbied for the standard.1 I find that the complexity of the adopted standard exacerbates new standards’ impairment of financial reporting quality.Third, I consider whether auditor-related factors affect the success of the adoption of standards. Auditors can provide assistance to their clients only insofar as they have available resources to increase staffing. Because standards implementation requires additional work, auditors generally attempt to allocate additional employees to affected clients. However, their ability to do so depends on the availability of additional auditors. I expect that offices with more clients concurrently adopting new standards will have fewer available personnel and be less successful in helping clients adopt the latest standards. Consistent with this expectation, I find that the negative effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated among offices that have more clients adopting new standards. I also find that the results are more pronounced for clients of non-Big 4 auditors, which is consistent with Big 4 auditors having more training and support resources, enabling more efficient audit program modifications.Finally, I conduct semi-structured interviews with financial statement preparers and audit partners to provide additional institutional context about how firms and their auditors collaborate to implement new standards.2 Interviewees note that the implementation of new standards requires significant effort and disrupts other processes and that firms often turn to their auditors for implementation guidance. Overall, the interviewees provide insights consistent with my empirical analyses.This study makes several contributions to the literature. While prior studies indicate certain prominent standards achieve targeted regulatory objectives, like improving inter-industry revenue comparability (Tillet, 2026), I find that the adoption of standards in general is associated with lower financial reporting quality. Importantly, the evidence suggests that new standards create a distraction effect that lowers financial reporting quality in areas unrelated to the standard being adopted. I also find that client, standard, and auditor-related factors influence the success of implementation. The FASB regularly conducts post-implementation reviews to examine unintended consequences or costs of standards, and these findings provide relevant feedback on the adoption process. This study suggests that one unintended consequence of a new standard is a negative effect on financial reporting quality in the year of adoption.Second, this study introduces a novel AI-based methodology to parse annual reports. Recent research across several streams of literature relies on various methodologies to glean insights from unstructured textual disclosures ranging from basic keyword searches to deep learning neural networks (see Bochkay et al., 2023 for a recent review). While some studies have begun using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) for identification (Bernard et al., 2026), this is the first study using a standard, publicly available LLM model for identification. Furthermore, while many studies examine the effects of accounting standards using financial statement ratios (Khan et al., 2018) or XBRL tags, my approach allows identification of standard adoption for any standard, so long as the impact is disclosed by the firm.Finally, this study contributes to the literature stream on employee workloads. Studies find that human capital resource constraints create higher workloads among employees, which influences disclosure quality (Chen et al., 2023). My study finds that standards likely to require more effort result in lower-quality financial reporting concentrated in the year of adoption. Prior research also investigates factors that increase auditor workload and finds that such increases harm audit quality (Bills et al., 2016; Czerney et al., 2019; Christensen et al., 2021a). This study finds that standards adoption increases auditor workload because auditors assist their clients with implementation, and the ability of an audit office to absorb the increased workload influences their clients’ success in adoption. proposed.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
proposed.abstract:
•
Accounting standards adoption leads to lower financial reporting quality.
•
Adopting firms are 31% more likely to misstate financial statements.
•
The misstatements are observable only in the year of adoption.
•
The misstatements involve areas unrelated to the new accounting standards.
•
Results are more pronounced in resource-constrained firms and auditors.

existing_records.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
existing_records.abstract: I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

after.title_zh: 应对新会计准则：对企业及其审计师的影响
after.abstract_zh: 我考察了实施新会计准则对财务报告质量的影响。尽管先前研究表明准则总体上实现了其监管目标，但近期文献发现企业面临显著的技术会计能力约束，这促使我们需要探究会计准则采用对财务报告质量更广泛的影响。我采用一种新颖的基于人工智能的方法来识别受新会计准则影响的企业，发现当企业实施新准则时，财务报告质量下降。证据表明，受损的财务报告质量出现在与新准则无关的会计领域，这与分心效应一致。当企业同时面临其他与会计相关的挑战、会计准则更为复杂以及审计师资源受限时，结果更为显著。这些发现为新会计准则的意外后果提供了证据，并为缓解这些成本的潜在途径提供了启示。

source_records.title: Measurement error when estimating covenant slack and violations
source_records.abstract: We collect quantitative (true thresholds and realizations) and qualitative (compliance status) covenant information from SEC filings to examine the accuracy of compliance estimates derived using data from commercial databases. Estimated covenant slack frequently overestimates covenant violations, and only rarely understates them, with this asymmetry holding for both qualitative and quantitative disclosers. The non-random structure of this measurement error has implications for research that relies on estimated violations or on precise measurement of covenant realizations near a threshold. Across our two samples of disclosers, we find evidence consistent with the debt covenant hypothesis for debt-to-EBITDA covenants once measurement error is considered. We also show that the lender forbearance rate declines sharply after correcting estimated violations for measurement error, and that true violations, but not estimated violations, are associated with negative stock market reactions and loan renegotiations. Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.

Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.
