By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.JEL classificationG21; M13; M4; O17KeywordsInformal economy; Developing economies; Microenterprises; Recordkeeping; Accounting quality; Financial inclusion; Access to creditIntroductionThis study examines the relationship between voluntary accounting practices and the informal economy in developing countries, where firms largely operate outside tax and business registrations, and beyond government enforcement (Ulyssea, 2020). We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. This unique setting allows us to observe accounting in its foundational role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance mechanism.5The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 examines when and why informal firms voluntarily keep systematic accounting records. Next, Section 3 explores how accounting quality relates to access to credit. Finally, Section 4 examines how accounting quality is associated with managerial decisions regarding microenterprise growth plans and productivity. fields.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

after.title_zh: 会计在非正规经济中的作用
after.abstract_zh: 我们利用来自危地马拉、洪都拉斯和萨尔瓦多1426家企业的全新调查数据，考察在非正规经济中经营的微型企业自愿采用会计系统的情况及其与获得信贷和业务增长之间的关联。尽管不存在监管强制要求，44%的非正规微型企业仍保留系统性财务记录，其中约四分之三使用笔记本，四分之一使用数字记录。会计质量与所有者的创业动机、财务投入和管理能力密切相关。依赖较大供应商、向客户提供分期信贷、开展营销促销或采用更正式组织结构的非正规企业，也更可能采用结构化记账系统，这凸显了会计作为管理工具的作用，而非作为合规职能或进入正规经济的前兆。保留将业务账户与个人账户分开的笔记本的非正规企业，显著更可能申请并获得银行贷款。我们对获得信贷的推断也适用于多米尼加共和国的微型企业。此外，会计质量似乎即使在非正规企业中也支持贷款人的尽职调查，尤其是当贷款人更为专业时。使用更广泛的信贷市场地位衡量指标，我们发现会计质量在各信贷层级之间单调上升。最后，我们发现拥有更高质量会计系统的企业家更可能规划业务扩张。通过阐明低执法环境下会计选择背后的动机，本研究加深了我们对会计在新兴市场早期业务发展中基础性作用的理解。

source_records.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets

This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. Formal tests confirm that the difference between the two treatments is significant, suggesting that adding methodological knowledge to the conceptual content is crucial for an effective intervention.Second, we examine whether our treatments mitigate the subsequent price reversal. Using the same DID framework, we find that treatment stocks indeed exhibit a smaller reversal than control stocks in both markets. For an average treatment stock, a one-standard-deviation increase in accruals improves the post-EA return by approximately 4.2% in China and 3.9% in the US relative to control stocks. As with the announcement-period results, this effect is concentrated in the group that received both conceptual and methodological knowledge: the negative relation between accruals and post-EA returns is essentially eliminated in this combined treatment group, whereas in the conceptual-only group the relation also improves but remains statistically insignificant. Together, the evidence indicates that the education treatment is effective in mitigating accrual mispricing and highlights the vital role of practical, methodological tools in this process.We obtain similar results when using unexpected discretionary accruals (see Balsam et al., 2002) and when using the comparison group as the benchmark in the DID analysis. A placebo test based on historical accruals yields no treatment effects, suggesting that our results are falsifiable. Additionally, we find that the treatment effects are more pronounced when the investors engage more with the educational materials (e.g., increased reading, comments, retweets, likes, and saves on our posts, as well as more clicks on the hyperlinks within the posts).Further analysis of the treatment effects indicates that these effects likely arise from addressing financial knowledge gaps among unsophisticated investors. First, the treatment effects are concentrated on stocks dominated by retail investors. Second, the education treatments reduce order imbalance (i.e., excessive purchases) for retail investors in stocks with high accruals on the EA day, but no similar pattern emerges for institutional investors. Third, the treatment effects are more pronounced in firms located in regions with low financial literacy.Lastly, we conduct tests to address alternative explanations. First, no education effect is found when comparing the control and comparison groups, negating the impact of treatment salience. Second, the education effect is evident only for positive accruals, aligning with our education's focus on high accrual implications and refuting the notion that our exercises merely amplify attention to accruals. Third, the education effect persists one year after the experiment, with no new messages posted, suggesting that our treatment effect is not fear-induced. Fourth, the effect remains pronounced in stocks with high trading turnover, implying a limited impact from the spillover effect due to common ownership between the treatment and control stocks. Finally, our results stay robust after accounting for the fixed effect of industry × EA months and excluding EAs during the pandemic peak, indicating minimal distortion from the COVID-19 outbreak.Our study makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on the effects of financial knowledge in financial markets. Existing studies mainly focus on the effects of financial knowledge on individuals’ financial decisions and behaviors (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to directly test the influence of financial knowledge on asset pricing.Second, our study extends research that examines financial anomalies and pricing efficiency. McLean and Pontiff (2016) posit that the academic discovery of financial anomalies can enhance market efficiency by enabling investors to pinpoint arbitrage opportunities. Our research underscores that not only is the discovery of such knowledge vital, but its dissemination and the education of investors regarding it are also crucial for improving market efficiency.Third, previous studies on accrual anomaly rest on explanations such as risk (Khan, 2008; Chichernea et al., 2015), transaction costs (Collins et al., 2003; Mashruwala et al., 2006), limited attention (Hirshleifer et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2016), and insufficient supplementary accounting information (Louis et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2016). We extend this body of literature by demonstrating a new explanation, namely investors’ limited understanding of accounting accruals. This perspective also sheds light on the understanding of other price anomalies.Lastly, our research carries policy implications. Individuals in many developed and developing countries have low levels of financial literacy (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Merkoulova and Veld, 2022). Although many financial education programs have been introduced worldwide to rectify this problem (Kaiser et al., 2022), their efficacy remains debatable (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Our findings underscore the potential of social media platforms as tools for investor education. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of integrating methodological applications with conceptual explanations in financial education. proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

before.title_zh: 知识就是力量：一项在中国和美国股票市场进行的实地实验
before.abstract_zh: 本研究考察金融知识对股票定价效率的因果效应。借助专门设计的投资者教育网站，我们开展了一项实地实验，在社交媒体上与中国和美国的投资者分享关于会计应计项目定价的见解。我们发现，相对于控制组股票，处理组股票的应计错误定价有所减少。当增强对应计项目概念性理解的知识与有助于应计项目定量应用的知识相结合时，这一效应尤为显著。此外，在投资者对教育内容参与更深但金融素养较低的股票中，处理效应更强。

This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. Formal tests confirm that the difference between the two treatments is significant, suggesting that adding methodological knowledge to the conceptual content is crucial for an effective intervention.Second, we examine whether our treatments mitigate the subsequent price reversal. Using the same DID framework, we find that treatment stocks indeed exhibit a smaller reversal than control stocks in both markets. For an average treatment stock, a one-standard-deviation increase in accruals improves the post-EA return by approximately 4.2% in China and 3.9% in the US relative to control stocks. As with the announcement-period results, this effect is concentrated in the group that received both conceptual and methodological knowledge: the negative relation between accruals and post-EA returns is essentially eliminated in this combined treatment group, whereas in the conceptual-only group the relation also improves but remains statistically insignificant. Together, the evidence indicates that the education treatment is effective in mitigating accrual mispricing and highlights the vital role of practical, methodological tools in this process.We obtain similar results when using unexpected discretionary accruals (see Balsam et al., 2002) and when using the comparison group as the benchmark in the DID analysis. A placebo test based on historical accruals yields no treatment effects, suggesting that our results are falsifiable. Additionally, we find that the treatment effects are more pronounced when the investors engage more with the educational materials (e.g., increased reading, comments, retweets, likes, and saves on our posts, as well as more clicks on the hyperlinks within the posts).Further analysis of the treatment effects indicates that these effects likely arise from addressing financial knowledge gaps among unsophisticated investors. First, the treatment effects are concentrated on stocks dominated by retail investors. Second, the education treatments reduce order imbalance (i.e., excessive purchases) for retail investors in stocks with high accruals on the EA day, but no similar pattern emerges for institutional investors. Third, the treatment effects are more pronounced in firms located in regions with low financial literacy.Lastly, we conduct tests to address alternative explanations. First, no education effect is found when comparing the control and comparison groups, negating the impact of treatment salience. Second, the education effect is evident only for positive accruals, aligning with our education's focus on high accrual implications and refuting the notion that our exercises merely amplify attention to accruals. Third, the education effect persists one year after the experiment, with no new messages posted, suggesting that our treatment effect is not fear-induced. Fourth, the effect remains pronounced in stocks with high trading turnover, implying a limited impact from the spillover effect due to common ownership between the treatment and control stocks. Finally, our results stay robust after accounting for the fixed effect of industry × EA months and excluding EAs during the pandemic peak, indicating minimal distortion from the COVID-19 outbreak.Our study makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on the effects of financial knowledge in financial markets. Existing studies mainly focus on the effects of financial knowledge on individuals’ financial decisions and behaviors (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to directly test the influence of financial knowledge on asset pricing.Second, our study extends research that examines financial anomalies and pricing efficiency. McLean and Pontiff (2016) posit that the academic discovery of financial anomalies can enhance market efficiency by enabling investors to pinpoint arbitrage opportunities. Our research underscores that not only is the discovery of such knowledge vital, but its dissemination and the education of investors regarding it are also crucial for improving market efficiency.Third, previous studies on accrual anomaly rest on explanations such as risk (Khan, 2008; Chichernea et al., 2015), transaction costs (Collins et al., 2003; Mashruwala et al., 2006), limited attention (Hirshleifer et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2016), and insufficient supplementary accounting information (Louis et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2016). We extend this body of literature by demonstrating a new explanation, namely investors’ limited understanding of accounting accruals. This perspective also sheds light on the understanding of other price anomalies.Lastly, our research carries policy implications. Individuals in many developed and developing countries have low levels of financial literacy (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Merkoulova and Veld, 2022). Although many financial education programs have been introduced worldwide to rectify this problem (Kaiser et al., 2022), their efficacy remains debatable (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Our findings underscore the potential of social media platforms as tools for investor education. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of integrating methodological applications with conceptual explanations in financial education. This insight holds considerable relevance for the design and execution of financial education programs.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literature“Financial knowledge,” or “financial literacy,” refers to people's ability to process economic information and make informed financial decisions (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

existing_records.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
existing_records.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

after.abstract_zh: 本研究考察金融知识对股票定价效率的因果效应。借助专门设计的投资者教育网站，我们开展了一项实地实验，在社交媒体上与中国和美国的投资者分享关于会计应计项目定价的见解。我们发现，相对于控制组股票，处理组股票的应计错误定价有所减少。当增强对应计项目概念性理解的知识与有助于应计项目定量应用的知识相结合时，这一效应尤为显著。此外，在投资者对教育内容参与更深但金融素养较低的股票中，处理效应更强。

source_records.title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
source_records.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.JEL classificationD22; D82; M40; M41KeywordsCorporate disclosure; Industry information; Peer information; Organization of firms; Delegation of decision rights; Managerial learning; Within-firm agency frictionsIntroductionDelegation is essential for firm growth and improves aggregate productivity (Bloom et al., 2012, Akcigit et al., 2021). However, less is known about industry- or country-wide mechanisms that facilitate or impede the delegation of decision rights from the CEO to division managers (DMs). This paper focuses on one such mechanism: the peer information environment, i.e., the industry information generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them. Specifically, I study whether the peer information environment in the division’s industry and country affects the delegation of decision rights over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales from the CEO to DMs.I build on theoretical models of delegation (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Dessein, 2002, Harris and Raviv, 2005) to develop my prediction about how peer information can affect delegation. A basic framework in these models involves a CEO who considers delegating decision rights (e.g., over capital investment and hiring) to a DM because the DM has superior local information about factors such as customer needs and investment opportunities (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992). However, when the preferences of the CEO and DM are not fully aligned, delegation allows the DM to act on their own preferences rather than the CEO’s, creating agency frictions (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). Thus, delegation increases when (i) the DM has a greater information advantage over the CEO and (ii) the incentives of the CEO and DM are better aligned. Peer information affects both the DM’s information advantage and agency frictions of delegation.First, peer information can affect the DM’s information advantage over the CEO. Decisions made by firms in the same industry (e.g., capital investment, hiring) are influenced by similar economic forces, such as common shocks to profitability and investment opportunities (Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000). Thus, disclosures by peer firms and coverage by information intermediaries can provide information (e.g., earnings forecasts and investment plans) relevant to understanding these common industry factors, helping managers make more informed decisions. Since peer information is available to both the CEO and DMs, its effect on delegation depends on who learns more from it. On the one hand, if the CEO gains more new information, the DM’s information advantage narrows, reducing the benefit of relying on the DM’s knowledge, and thus reducing delegation (CEO learning channel). On the other hand, a richer peer information environment can increase delegation if the DM learns more. Garicano (2000) develops a theoretical model that relaxes the assumption that the DM has an information advantage and shows that delegation increases when more information becomes available, enabling DMs to acquire – at a lower cost – the knowledge needed to make informed decisions (DM learning channel).Second, peer information reduces agency frictions of delegation by helping the CEO better evaluate and monitor DMs (agency mitigation channel). For example, CEOs can use peer information to obtain relevant information about the costs of production, profitability, and investment expenditures in the industry, all of which provide useful benchmarks for filtering common shocks out of DMs’ performance and for monitoring DMs (Holmstrom, 1982, Nalebuff and Stiglitz, 1983, Cichello et al., 2009). Thus, the agency mitigation channel predicts that richer peer information reduces agency costs of delegation, motivating the CEO to increase delegation.To summarize, peer information can affect delegation through three channels. The agency mitigation and DM learning channels predict that a richer peer information environment increases delegation, whereas the CEO learning channel predicts the opposite. Thus, whether peer information increases or decreases delegation is ultimately an empirical question.Studying delegation within firms is challenging because it is largely unobservable to researchers (e.g., Prendergast, 2002). To overcome this challenge, I obtain information on the internal organization of firms using an international dataset from several waves of the World Management Survey (WMS) (Bloom et al., 2012, Scur et al., 2021). The WMS surveys a large number of randomly selected medium-sized public and private firms in North and South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. The WMS data are obtained through in-depth interviews with DMs using interview questions designed to be directly applicable to the theories of delegation discussed above (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). To measure the degree of delegation, I use the WMS data on DMs’ authority over four decisions: capital investment, hiring, investment in new products, and sales. The interviews are performed with one DM per firm. In addition to data on the degree of delegation, the WMS data include detailed information on the DM, division, and firm characteristics.To measure the richness of the peer information environment, I rely on prior research (Holmstrom, 1982, Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000, Shroff et al., 2017) and construct a proxy that captures (i) the relevance (i.e., informativeness) of peer information for understanding common industry factors and (ii) the aggregate amount of peer information available about these factors. To proxy for the relevance of peer information within an industry, I use the degree of earnings synchronicity in the industry. My intuition is that, when a peer firm’s earnings synchronicity is high, its earnings co-move more closely with industry-wide economic conditions, making its disclosures more informative about the common factors that also affect the focal firm’s division. I measure the aggregate amount of peer information using two proxies. The first proxy is the analyst coverage of peer firms in the industry (measured as the average number of analysts per peer firm). Prior research shows that analysts are industry experts who not only supply firm-specific and industry-level information through their reports (Brown et al., 2015), but also demand greater quantity and quality of disclosures from the firms they cover (Irani and Oesch, 2013, Christensen et al., 2021), thereby improving the peer information environment. My second proxy for the aggregate amount of peer information is the press coverage of peer firms. The press disseminates firm-initiated disclosures and produces new information through journalism (e.g., Bushee et al., 2010), enhancing the peer information environment. I calculate these three proxies by averaging across all firms in the division’s industry and country, excluding the focal firm. I then convert each proxy into a within-country quartile rank and average the three ranked proxies to construct my measure of the peer information environment.I test the relation between peer information and delegation using an international sample of 4908 unique public and private firms with 6663 firm-year observations over the 2005–2015 period. I find that firms with richer peer information delegate more, using a model that includes time-varying division-, firm-, and industry-level control variables that might affect delegation (e.g., firm size, incentive contracts, and internal information quality) as well as year×industry and year×country fixed effects. In terms of economic magnitude, an increase of one within-fixed effects standard deviation in peer information (resp. moving from the average firm in China to the average firm in the US) is associated with a 4% (resp. 13%) within-fixed effects standard deviation increase in delegation. These economic magnitudes are comparable to those reported by Bloom et al. (2012), who find that a one standard deviation increase in social trust is associated with a 7% standard deviation increase in delegation. My results are robust to alternative peer information measures and fixed effect structures.Next, I use three sets of tests to explore the potential channels underlying the relation between peer information and delegation: agency mitigation, CEO learning, and DM learning. First, I explore the agency mitigation channel. If peer information mitigates agency costs, its effect on delegation should be stronger when agency problems of delegation are greater. I explore two alternative mechanisms that mitigate agency problems: social trust and product market competition. When the CEO trusts the DM to act in the CEO’s interest, the agency frictions of delegation are lower. Consistent with this, Bloom et al. (2012) find that CEOs in high-trust regions delegate more. Similarly, DMs operating in competitive industries have stronger incentives to work hard and improve their performance because they have little slack (Bloom et al., 2010). Thus, these mechanisms reduce the need to monitor the DM. However, when these alternative mechanisms are weak, the importance of peer information for resolving agency frictions increases. Consistent with the agency mitigation channel, my results show that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when trust in the CEO’s region is lower and when competition in the DM’s industry is less intense.Second, I examine the CEO learning channel. The basic idea is that, if peer information affects delegation through CEO learning, its effect should vary with the CEO’s information set, e.g., a less informed CEO is more likely to learn from peer information. Although the CEO’s information set is not directly observable, I build on prior research and use proxies based on the CEO’s prior industry experience and tenure. Several studies document that greater industry experience and firm tenure lead to more informed decisions and reduce managers’ reliance on external information sources for learning (e.g., Cici et al., 2018, Guo and Zhong, 2023). These studies suggest that CEOs with less industry experience and shorter tenure are less informed and, therefore, more likely to learn from peer firms than those with extensive experience and longer tenure. Consistent with the CEO learning channel, which predicts that CEO learning reduces delegation, I find that the relation between peer information and delegation becomes negative when CEOs have less industry experience and when they have shorter tenure (i.e., when CEO learning is more likely).Third, I explore the DM learning channel using an idea similar to the one used for the CEO learning channel. If peer information impacts delegation by facilitating DM learning, its effect should depend on the DM’s information set, e.g., a less informed DM is more likely to learn from peer information. I use the DM’s tenure as a proxy for how informed the DM would be about the division and its industry absent peer information. A newly hired DM is less likely to possess extensive knowledge about the division’s operations. As DMs’ tenure increases, they acquire a deeper understanding of the division’s operations, industry dynamics, and how these industry-level factors impact the division. Thus, a DM with shorter tenure is more likely to learn from peer information. Consistent with the DM learning channel, which predicts that DM learning motivates the CEO to delegate more, I find that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when DMs have shorter tenure.Examining the peer information environment rather than the firm’s own can mitigate concerns that the firm endogenously determines both delegation and its information environment. However, the peer effects literature faces its own empirical challenges (Manski, 1993; Section 4.6.2 Angrist and Pischke, 2009). A standard concern in this literature is that common characteristics or shocks may drive both peers’ and the focal firm’s outcomes, leading to omitted variable bias. For instance, consider an industry-wide shock to investment opportunities (e.g., a technological innovation). Firms in the industry, both the focal firm and its peers, may respond by (i) investing and growing larger, which can motivate greater delegation, and (ii) raising external capital to fund these investments, which can motivate greater disclosure to facilitate this financing. Thus, the common shock can increase both the focal firm’s delegation and peer disclosure, generating a positive association between the two even in the absence of any causal effect.I take several steps to mitigate such endogeneity concerns. First, I find that the results are robust to including a battery of control variables as well as year×industry, year×country, and industry×country fixed effects. Second, using the test developed by Oster (2019), I find that, to move the estimated effect to zero, omitted variables would need to be 5.69 times as important as my control variables, which seems unlikely. Third, and more importantly, I employ an alternative identification strategy using a simulated instrument that exploits threshold-induced variation in the extent of financial reporting requirements across industries in Europe (Breuer, 2021, Breuer, 2025). Using this instrument, I find that mandating a greater share of firms in an industry to disclose their financial statements increases delegation within firms in that industry.This paper makes several contributions. My study relates to the empirical literature on the factors influencing the internal allocation of decision rights. This literature links delegation to social trust (Bloom et al., 2012); personal characteristics of the CEO and characteristics of the decision (Graham et al., 2015); a firm’s own organizational design, information technology, and predictive analytics (e.g., Baiman et al., 1995, Abernethy et al., 2004, Indjejikian and Matejka, 2012, Bloom et al., 2014, Labro et al., 2023); and the firm’s operating environment (e.g., Acemoglu et al., 2007, Campbell et al., 2009, Bloom et al., 2010, Robinson and Stocken, 2013).1 My study contributes to this literature in two ways: (i) I propose external financial reporting and disclosure as a mechanism that facilitates delegation; and (ii) I extend the prior research exploring mechanisms that reduce agency frictions of delegation within firms, including incentive contracts in Abernethy et al. (2004) and social trust in Bloom et al. (2012), by documenting that a richer information environment reduces these frictions.In addition, this paper relates to the literature examining the real effects of financial reporting and disclosure, particularly on investment decisions.2 My study extends this literature in two ways. First, in their review of the real effects literature, Roychowdhury et al. (2019) note, “Overall, it appears that most of the literature has concentrated on classic agency frictions arising from manager-shareholder conflicts, whereas other agency conflicts have received less attention” [emphasis added]. I extend the literature by documenting that peer information increases delegation by reducing agency conflicts within firms between the CEO and DMs. Shroff et al. (2014) also explore agency frictions between the parent and subsidiaries within multinational companies by examining capital investment efficiency. I complement their study by exploring the effects of peer information on delegation within firms. Second, Labro and Pierk (2026) highlight that most studies in this literature document the effects of financial reporting on corporate decisions (e.g., capital investment) but provide limited direct evidence on the management (accounting) practices that support those decisions, likely because such practices are generally unobservable to researchers. My study answers their call for more direct evidence by examining one such management practice: the delegation of decision rights within firms, which can lead to more informed decisions (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992).Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsPeer information environment and delegationTheoretical work exploring the delegation of decision rights from the principal (CEO in my setting) to the agent (DM in my setting) highlights (i) the efficiency of using the local information dispersed among individuals and (ii) the agency frictions of delegating decision rights (e.g., Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992, Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Harris and Raviv, 2005). proposed.title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
proposed.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

before.title_zh: 企业内部的管理层授权与同行信息环境
before.abstract_zh: 本文考察同行信息环境——由同行企业的披露以及覆盖这些企业的信息中介所产生——是否以及如何影响CEO将决策权授予部门经理（DM）。利用一个国际调查数据集，我衡量了企业在资本投资、人力资本投资、新产品投资和销售方面决策的內部授权程度。我发现，在同行信息环境更丰富的国家-行业中，CEO会向部门经理授予更多权力。横截面检验凸显了三个潜在渠道。具体而言，结果表明，同行信息（i）帮助CEO获取信息，以减少相对于DM的潜在信息劣势（CEO学习），（ii）缓解CEO-DM代理摩擦（代理缓解），以及（iii）为DM提供相关信息以做出更好的决策（DM学习）。虽然CEO学习会减少授权，但代理缓解和DM学习会增加授权。这些发现提供了证据，表明关于同行的信息会影响企业的内部组织。
