Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.JEL classificationD22; D82; M40; M41KeywordsCorporate disclosure; Industry information; Peer information; Organization of firms; Delegation of decision rights; Managerial learning; Within-firm agency frictionsIntroductionDelegation is essential for firm growth and improves aggregate productivity (Bloom et al., 2012, Akcigit et al., 2021). However, less is known about industry- or country-wide mechanisms that facilitate or impede the delegation of decision rights from the CEO to division managers (DMs). This paper focuses on one such mechanism: the peer information environment, i.e., the industry information generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them. Specifically, I study whether the peer information environment in the division’s industry and country affects the delegation of decision rights over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales from the CEO to DMs.I build on theoretical models of delegation (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997, Dessein, 2002, Harris and Raviv, 2005) to develop my prediction about how peer information can affect delegation. A basic framework in these models involves a CEO who considers delegating decision rights (e.g., over capital investment and hiring) to a DM because the DM has superior local information about factors such as customer needs and investment opportunities (Hayek, 1945, Jensen and Meckling, 1992). However, when the preferences of the CEO and DM are not fully aligned, delegation allows the DM to act on their own preferences rather than the CEO’s, creating agency frictions (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). Thus, delegation increases when (i) the DM has a greater information advantage over the CEO and (ii) the incentives of the CEO and DM are better aligned. Peer information affects both the DM’s information advantage and agency frictions of delegation.First, peer information can affect the DM’s information advantage over the CEO. Decisions made by firms in the same industry (e.g., capital investment, hiring) are influenced by similar economic forces, such as common shocks to profitability and investment opportunities (Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000). Thus, disclosures by peer firms and coverage by information intermediaries can provide information (e.g., earnings forecasts and investment plans) relevant to understanding these common industry factors, helping managers make more informed decisions. Since peer information is available to both the CEO and DMs, its effect on delegation depends on who learns more from it. On the one hand, if the CEO gains more new information, the DM’s information advantage narrows, reducing the benefit of relying on the DM’s knowledge, and thus reducing delegation (CEO learning channel). On the other hand, a richer peer information environment can increase delegation if the DM learns more. Garicano (2000) develops a theoretical model that relaxes the assumption that the DM has an information advantage and shows that delegation increases when more information becomes available, enabling DMs to acquire – at a lower cost – the knowledge needed to make informed decisions (DM learning channel).Second, peer information reduces agency frictions of delegation by helping the CEO better evaluate and monitor DMs (agency mitigation channel). For example, CEOs can use peer information to obtain relevant information about the costs of production, profitability, and investment expenditures in the industry, all of which provide useful benchmarks for filtering common shocks out of DMs’ performance and for monitoring DMs (Holmstrom, 1982, Nalebuff and Stiglitz, 1983, Cichello et al., 2009). Thus, the agency mitigation channel predicts that richer peer information reduces agency costs of delegation, motivating the CEO to increase delegation.To summarize, peer information can affect delegation through three channels. The agency mitigation and DM learning channels predict that a richer peer information environment increases delegation, whereas the CEO learning channel predicts the opposite. Thus, whether peer information increases or decreases delegation is ultimately an empirical question.Studying delegation within firms is challenging because it is largely unobservable to researchers (e.g., Prendergast, 2002). To overcome this challenge, I obtain information on the internal organization of firms using an international dataset from several waves of the World Management Survey (WMS) (Bloom et al., 2012, Scur et al., 2021). The WMS surveys a large number of randomly selected medium-sized public and private firms in North and South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. The WMS data are obtained through in-depth interviews with DMs using interview questions designed to be directly applicable to the theories of delegation discussed above (e.g., Aghion and Tirole, 1997). To measure the degree of delegation, I use the WMS data on DMs’ authority over four decisions: capital investment, hiring, investment in new products, and sales. The interviews are performed with one DM per firm. In addition to data on the degree of delegation, the WMS data include detailed information on the DM, division, and firm characteristics.To measure the richness of the peer information environment, I rely on prior research (Holmstrom, 1982, Admati and Pfleiderer, 2000, Shroff et al., 2017) and construct a proxy that captures (i) the relevance (i.e., informativeness) of peer information for understanding common industry factors and (ii) the aggregate amount of peer information available about these factors. To proxy for the relevance of peer information within an industry, I use the degree of earnings synchronicity in the industry. My intuition is that, when a peer firm’s earnings synchronicity is high, its earnings co-move more closely with industry-wide economic conditions, making its disclosures more informative about the common factors that also affect the focal firm’s division. I measure the aggregate amount of peer information using two proxies. The first proxy is the analyst coverage of peer firms in the industry (measured as the average number of analysts per peer firm). Prior research shows that analysts are industry experts who not only supply firm-specific and industry-level information through their reports (Brown et al., 2015), but also demand greater quantity and quality of disclosures from the firms they cover (Irani and Oesch, 2013, Christensen et al., 2021), thereby improving the peer information environment. My second proxy for the aggregate amount of peer information is the press coverage of peer firms. The press disseminates firm-initiated disclosures and produces new information through journalism (e.g., Bushee et al., 2010), enhancing the peer information environment. I calculate these three proxies by averaging across all firms in the division’s industry and country, excluding the focal firm. I then convert each proxy into a within-country quartile rank and average the three ranked proxies to construct my measure of the peer information environment.I test the relation between peer information and delegation using an international sample of 4908 unique public and private firms with 6663 firm-year observations over the 2005–2015 period. I find that firms with richer peer information delegate more, using a model that includes time-varying division-, firm-, and industry-level control variables that might affect delegation (e.g., firm size, incentive contracts, and internal information quality) as well as year×industry and year×country fixed effects. In terms of economic magnitude, an increase of one within-fixed effects standard deviation in peer information (resp. moving from the average firm in China to the average firm in the US) is associated with a 4% (resp. 13%) within-fixed effects standard deviation increase in delegation. These economic magnitudes are comparable to those reported by Bloom et al. (2012), who find that a one standard deviation increase in social trust is associated with a 7% standard deviation increase in delegation. My results are robust to alternative peer information measures and fixed effect structures.Next, I use three sets of tests to explore the potential channels underlying the relation between peer information and delegation: agency mitigation, CEO learning, and DM learning. First, I explore the agency mitigation channel. If peer information mitigates agency costs, its effect on delegation should be stronger when agency problems of delegation are greater. I explore two alternative mechanisms that mitigate agency problems: social trust and product market competition. When the CEO trusts the DM to act in the CEO’s interest, the agency frictions of delegation are lower. Consistent with this, Bloom et al. (2012) find that CEOs in high-trust regions delegate more. Similarly, DMs operating in competitive industries have stronger incentives to work hard and improve their performance because they have little slack (Bloom et al., 2010). Thus, these mechanisms reduce the need to monitor the DM. However, when these alternative mechanisms are weak, the importance of peer information for resolving agency frictions increases. Consistent with the agency mitigation channel, my results show that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when trust in the CEO’s region is lower and when competition in the DM’s industry is less intense.Second, I examine the CEO learning channel. The basic idea is that, if peer information affects delegation through CEO learning, its effect should vary with the CEO’s information set, e.g., a less informed CEO is more likely to learn from peer information. Although the CEO’s information set is not directly observable, I build on prior research and use proxies based on the CEO’s prior industry experience and tenure. Several studies document that greater industry experience and firm tenure lead to more informed decisions and reduce managers’ reliance on external information sources for learning (e.g., Cici et al., 2018, Guo and Zhong, 2023). These studies suggest that CEOs with less industry experience and shorter tenure are less informed and, therefore, more likely to learn from peer firms than those with extensive experience and longer tenure. Consistent with the CEO learning channel, which predicts that CEO learning reduces delegation, I find that the relation between peer information and delegation becomes negative when CEOs have less industry experience and when they have shorter tenure (i.e., when CEO learning is more likely).Third, I explore the DM learning channel using an idea similar to the one used for the CEO learning channel. If peer information impacts delegation by facilitating DM learning, its effect should depend on the DM’s information set, e.g., a less informed DM is more likely to learn from peer information. I use the DM’s tenure as a proxy for how informed the DM would be about the division and its industry absent peer information. A newly hired DM is less likely to possess extensive knowledge about the division’s operations. As DMs’ tenure increases, they acquire a deeper understanding of the division’s operations, industry dynamics, and how these industry-level factors impact the division. Thus, a DM with shorter tenure is more likely to learn from peer information. Consistent with the DM learning channel, which predicts that DM learning motivates the CEO to delegate more, I find that the positive relation between peer information and delegation is stronger when DMs have shorter tenure.Examining the peer information environment rather than the firm’s own can mitigate concerns that the firm endogenously determines both delegation and its information environment. proposed.title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
proposed.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

after.title_zh: 企业内部的管理层授权与同行信息环境
after.abstract_zh: 本文考察同行信息环境——由同行企业的披露以及覆盖这些企业的信息中介所产生——是否以及如何影响CEO将决策权授予部门经理（DM）。利用一个国际调查数据集，我衡量了企业在资本投资、人力资本投资、新产品投资和销售方面决策的內部授权程度。我发现，在同行信息环境更丰富的国家-行业中，CEO会向部门经理授予更多权力。横截面检验凸显了三个潜在渠道。具体而言，结果表明，同行信息（i）帮助CEO获取信息，以减少相对于DM的潜在信息劣势（CEO学习），（ii）缓解CEO-DM代理摩擦（代理缓解），以及（iii）为DM提供相关信息以做出更好的决策（DM学习）。虽然CEO学习会减少授权，但代理缓解和DM学习会增加授权。这些发现提供了证据，表明关于同行的信息会影响企业的内部组织。

source_records.title: Direct and Indirect Effects of Transparency Regulation
source_records.abstract: We examine the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation on economic activity. Using two distinct sources of regulatory variation—the varying extent of financial-reporting requirements and the staggered introduction of electronic business registers in Europe—, we find that direct exposure to transparency regulation tends to hurt focal firms’ economic activity (e.g., production and employment). By contrast, we find that indirect exposure to transparency regulation imposed on other related firms tends to help focal firms’ economic activity. In terms of relative magnitudes, we find that the negative direct and positive indirect effects tend to be of similar size, almost perfectly offsetting each other. Collectively, our evidence suggests that transparency regulation appears to primarily reallocate economic activity from more toward less regulated markets rather than help or hurt aggregate economic activity.

Using two distinct sources of regulatory variation—the varying extent of financial-reporting requirements and the staggered introduction of electronic business registers in Europe—, we find that direct exposure to transparency regulation tends to hurt focal firms’ economic activity (e.g., production and employment). By contrast, we find that indirect exposure to transparency regulation imposed on other related firms tends to help focal firms’ economic activity. Collectively, our evidence suggests that transparency regulation appears to primarily reallocate economic activity from more toward less regulated markets rather than help or hurt aggregate economic activity.KeywordsRegulation; Reallocation; Transparency; Disclosure; Supply ChainJEL Codes: K22; L51; M21; M41; M481. IntroductionRegulators around the world subject millions of firms to transparency requirements, albeit to varying extents. The leading economic rationale for these regulatory interventions is that firms’ transparency comes with positive economy-wide externalities (e.g., Leuz, 2010; Minnis and Shroff, 2017). Positive externalities imply that indirect benefits enjoyed by all firms resulting from some regulated firms’ transparency (e.g., improved investment decisions of peer firms) exceed the direct costs imposed on the regulated firms. Evidence on the relative importance of the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation, however, remains elusive. Two notable challenges contribute to this state of the literature. For one, it is notoriously difficult to comprehensively capture the various direct and especially indirect effects that transparency regulation unfolds. For another, and relatedly, it is challenging to aggregate and compare the rich evidence on regulatory effects in the literature given that individual studies vary in the effects they estimate, the samples of firms they use, the regulatory interventions they exploit, and the outcomes they study.In this study, we jointly estimate the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation to make progress toward understanding the relative importance of these effects. Building on Berg et al. (2021), we develop an empirical approach that allows disentangling and comparing the direct and indirect effects. Our approach exhibits two crucial features. First, it includes both the extent to which focal firms are subject to transparency regulation and the extent to which other firms are subject to the regulation as treatment variables in one regression. This feature allows separating the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation on focal firms and facilitates comparing the relative sizes of these distinct effects. Second, our approach uses first-order measures of aggregate economic activity, such as production, capital, and employment at the industry level, as outcomes. This feature helps comprehensively incorporate and summarize various costs and benefits of transparency regulation incurred by millions of firms, including unregulated firms.The signs and relative magnitudes of the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation are informative about the effectiveness of regulation (e.g., Dávila and Walther, 2021). If both effects are positive (negative), regulation unambiguously helps (hurts) economic activity. If, by contrast, the direct and indirect effects exhibit opposite signs, regulation reallocates economic activity. The direction of this reallocation depends on the sign combination: a positive direct effect and negative indirect effect would imply a reallocation toward regulated markets, whereas a negative direct effect and positive indirect effect would imply a reallocation away from regulated markets. The extent of this reallocation and, ultimately, the effectiveness of transparency regulation depends on the relative magnitudes of the effects. If the effects are of similar (absolute) size, any positive indirect effect would essentially be a transfer from regulated to unregulated firms, not a (net) positive externality. If the positive indirect effect, instead, outweighs any direct negative effects, we would have evidence of a positive externality—a potential reason to regulate.From extant literature, the signs and relative magnitudes of the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation remain unclear. The literature provides evidence of both benefits (e.g., capital-market benefits) and costs (e.g., proprietary costs) incurred by firms because of their required transparency. Similarly, the literature provides evidence of both benefits (e.g., due to information spillovers) and costs (e.g., due to general equilibrium forces) incurred by firms because of other firms’ required transparency. Accordingly, it is difficult to infer the ultimate signs and relative sizes of the (aggregate) direct and indirect effects, leaving open important questions about the effectiveness of transparency regulation and the existence and importance of any resulting positive externalities.We examine the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation in the context of the European financial-reporting regulation. The EU Accounting Directives require limited-liability firms to publicly disclose a full set of financial statements. To reduce the regulatory burden for smaller private firms, the directives grant exemptions from full reporting requirements for firms below firm-size thresholds. The thresholds vary across countries in the EU (Minnis and Shroff, 2017), providing notable variation in the extent of reporting regulation. Similar variation exists in countries’ implementation timing of centralized electronic business registers, which facilitate the dissemination of firms’ financial statements. The EU required its member countries to implement such electronic registers by January 1st of 2007 at the latest, but the actual introduction dates vary across countries.We exploit the variation in exemption thresholds and business registers to identify the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation. before.title_zh: 透明度监管的直接效应与间接效应
before.abstract_zh: 我们考察透明度监管对经济活动的直接效应与间接效应。利用两种不同的监管变异来源——财务报告要求的程度差异以及欧洲电子企业登记册的分阶段引入——，我们发现，直接暴露于透明度监管往往会损害焦点企业的经济活动（例如生产和就业）。相比之下，我们发现，由施加于其他关联企业的透明度监管所带来的间接暴露，往往有助于焦点企业的经济活动。就相对幅度而言，我们发现负向直接效应与正向间接效应往往规模相近，几乎完全相互抵消。总体而言，我们的证据表明，透明度监管似乎主要是将经济活动从监管较多的市场重新配置到监管较少的市场，而非帮助或损害总体经济活动。

IntroductionRegulators around the world subject millions of firms to transparency requirements, albeit to varying extents. The leading economic rationale for these regulatory interventions is that firms’ transparency comes with positive economy-wide externalities (e.g., Leuz, 2010; Minnis and Shroff, 2017). Positive externalities imply that indirect benefits enjoyed by all firms resulting from some regulated firms’ transparency (e.g., improved investment decisions of peer firms) exceed the direct costs imposed on the regulated firms. Evidence on the relative importance of the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation, however, remains elusive. Two notable challenges contribute to this state of the literature. For one, it is notoriously difficult to comprehensively capture the various direct and especially indirect effects that transparency regulation unfolds. For another, and relatedly, it is challenging to aggregate and compare the rich evidence on regulatory effects in the literature given that individual studies vary in the effects they estimate, the samples of firms they use, the regulatory interventions they exploit, and the outcomes they study.In this study, we jointly estimate the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation to make progress toward understanding the relative importance of these effects. Building on Berg et al. (2021), we develop an empirical approach that allows disentangling and comparing the direct and indirect effects. Our approach exhibits two crucial features. First, it includes both the extent to which focal firms are subject to transparency regulation and the extent to which other firms are subject to the regulation as treatment variables in one regression. This feature allows separating the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation on focal firms and facilitates comparing the relative sizes of these distinct effects. Second, our approach uses first-order measures of aggregate economic activity, such as production, capital, and employment at the industry level, as outcomes. This feature helps comprehensively incorporate and summarize various costs and benefits of transparency regulation incurred by millions of firms, including unregulated firms.The signs and relative magnitudes of the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation are informative about the effectiveness of regulation (e.g., Dávila and Walther, 2021). If both effects are positive (negative), regulation unambiguously helps (hurts) economic activity. If, by contrast, the direct and indirect effects exhibit opposite signs, regulation reallocates economic activity. The direction of this reallocation depends on the sign combination: a positive direct effect and negative indirect effect would imply a reallocation toward regulated markets, whereas a negative direct effect and positive indirect effect would imply a reallocation away from regulated markets. The extent of this reallocation and, ultimately, the effectiveness of transparency regulation depends on the relative magnitudes of the effects. If the effects are of similar (absolute) size, any positive indirect effect would essentially be a transfer from regulated to unregulated firms, not a (net) positive externality. If the positive indirect effect, instead, outweighs any direct negative effects, we would have evidence of a positive externality—a potential reason to regulate.From extant literature, the signs and relative magnitudes of the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation remain unclear. The literature provides evidence of both benefits (e.g., capital-market benefits) and costs (e.g., proprietary costs) incurred by firms because of their required transparency. Similarly, the literature provides evidence of both benefits (e.g., due to information spillovers) and costs (e.g., due to general equilibrium forces) incurred by firms because of other firms’ required transparency. after.title_zh: 透明度监管的直接效应与间接效应
after.abstract_zh: 我们考察透明度监管对经济活动的直接效应与间接效应。利用两种不同的监管变异来源——财务报告要求的程度差异以及欧洲电子企业登记册的分阶段引入——，我们发现，直接暴露于透明度监管往往会损害焦点企业的经济活动（例如生产和就业）。相比之下，我们发现，由施加于其他关联企业的透明度监管所带来的间接暴露，往往有助于焦点企业的经济活动。就相对幅度而言，我们发现负向直接效应与正向间接效应往往规模相近，几乎完全相互抵消。总体而言，我们的证据表明，透明度监管似乎主要是将经济活动从监管较多的市场重新配置到监管较少的市场，而非帮助或损害总体经济活动。

source_records.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
source_records.abstract: I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.KeywordsAccounting standards; Financial reporting quality; Audit quality; Resource constraintsJEL classificationM41; M42; M49IntroductionSince the Accounting Standard Codification (ASC) project launched in 2009, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) has issued more than 200 accounting standards updates (ASUs). Most new standards include a section titled “Benefits and Costs,” where the FASB justifies the potential increased cost of financial statement preparation with the additional benefit of improved information quality. Prior research has provided insights about the effects of specific, prominent standards (e.g., Henry et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2019; Tillet, 2026), but there is a paucity of evidence about whether and to what extent FASB standards satisfy the FASB's intent noted in each standard. As prominent standards examined in other studies often involve sweeping changes and are not representative of typical standards, our understanding of the influence of new standards on financial reporting quality is limited. Recent research indicates that firms have limited accounting expertise (Huang et al., 2025) and their behavior toward the typical standard differs from their preparation for prominent standards (e.g., revenue), which suggests that firms may not have available resources to implement new standards. In this study, I examine how new accounting standards affect financial reporting quality and which factors moderate this relationship.Despite more than 15 standards, on average, becoming effective each year, prior studies provide few details about the challenges firms and their auditors face during implementation. Yet, adopting new standards has the potential to affect financial reporting quality for several reasons. Firms often must re-evaluate their existing procedures, implement new IT systems, or hire additional personnel. In addition, adoption increases the workload for both preparers and their auditors, and both groups’ performance declines under such conditions (Chen et al., 2023; Christensen et al., 2021a). Given the ongoing accounting resource strains (AICPA, 2023) and the difficulty investors face when standards change (Dyer et al., 2025), it is important to understand how the implementation of standards influences financial reporting quality.To conduct my empirical analyses, I must identify which firms are affected by new accounting standards. This task is challenging due to varying language and disclosure choices among adopting firms. Prior studies have addressed this challenge by focusing on a single, prominent standard that produced an observable financial statement effect (e.g., Hunsader et al., 2022) or by identifying the types of firms likely affected by a single, new standard (e.g., Khan et al., 2018). As my analysis investigates the effects across all new standards, I develop a new method to identify affected firms. That is, I use a novel AI-based tool to parse more than 50,000 XBRL disclosures and identify firms adopting any standard that materially affects their financial statements. I then examine how standards adoption affects firms’ financial reporting quality.I find that adoption occurs frequently and that it negatively influences the quality of financial reporting. Approximately 37 percent of firm years across my sample are involved in the adoption of a new standard that has a material impact. Moreover, I find that adopting firms are 31 percent more likely to restate their annual filings through an item 4.02 disclosure (Big R restatements) and 44 percent more likely to fail to disclose an existing material weakness than firms unaffected by a new standard. Thus, new standards appear to have an immediate, detrimental effect on financial reporting quality.To better understand how standards adoption harms financial reporting quality, I examine two potential drivers of this effect. First, the firm may face challenges in implementing the standard's requirements, resulting in improper reporting about the subject matter of the standard. With a new standard, firms may not have pertinent expertise or resources to implement the standard without error. Alternatively, firms and their auditors likely recognize the possibility of increased regulatory scrutiny of areas affected by the standard, so they may devote sufficient effort to ensure those areas are reported properly. However, this increased attention may draw resources away from other financial reporting areas, resulting in lower financial reporting quality in areas unaffected by new standards (Kahneman, 1973; Seidel, 2017).To test these competing explanations, I examine the restatement categories associated with standards adoption. I find that the detrimental effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated in accounting areas unrelated to the new standard and completed late in the audit. I corroborate these findings with SEC comment letters. I find that firms adopting new standards are 6.5 percent more likely to receive an SEC comment letter, but I fail to find evidence that these comment letters reference the new standards. Results from these tests suggest that standards adoption diverts firm and auditor attention to the new standard and away from other areas. To corroborate this inference, I examine the duration of this effect. If the impairment stems from a diversion of firm and auditor resources during the adoption, the effect will likely dissipate after the adoption is completed. I find that the reduction in financial reporting quality is evident only in the year of adoption. Collectively, the evidence suggests that the adoption of a new accounting standard is associated with a decrease in financial reporting quality that is concentrated in the adoption year in areas unrelated to the standard itself.I expect that the effect on financial reporting quality differs based on firm, standard, and auditor characteristics, so I next test how these factors influence its magnitude. Regarding firm-level factors, recent research (Huang et al., 2025) suggests that firms often lack sufficient internal accounting expertise to handle increases in workloads that may be required to adopt a standard. I find that financial reporting quality impairments are more pronounced when firms are in unregulated industries, have ongoing mergers, experience accounting personnel turnover, or have existing internal control deficiencies. Collectively, this evidence suggests that concurrent accounting-related challenges influence the effect of adopting new accounting standards.Second, I investigate standard-level factors that may influence the success of adoption. Accounting standards vary in their scope, with some simply modifying minor disclosure requirements while others require significant accounting policy changes. More complex standards are more likely to require additional work from firms and their auditors, which may lead to lower financial reporting quality. I use three proxies for standards complexity: the FOG index, the length of the standard, and the degree to which auditors lobbied for the standard.1 I find that the complexity of the adopted standard exacerbates new standards’ impairment of financial reporting quality.Third, I consider whether auditor-related factors affect the success of the adoption of standards. Auditors can provide assistance to their clients only insofar as they have available resources to increase staffing. Because standards implementation requires additional work, auditors generally attempt to allocate additional employees to affected clients. However, their ability to do so depends on the availability of additional auditors. I expect that offices with more clients concurrently adopting new standards will have fewer available personnel and be less successful in helping clients adopt the latest standards. Consistent with this expectation, I find that the negative effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated among offices that have more clients adopting new standards. I also find that the results are more pronounced for clients of non-Big 4 auditors, which is consistent with Big 4 auditors having more training and support resources, enabling more efficient audit program modifications.Finally, I conduct semi-structured interviews with financial statement preparers and audit partners to provide additional institutional context about how firms and their auditors collaborate to implement new standards.2 Interviewees note that the implementation of new standards requires significant effort and disrupts other processes and that firms often turn to their auditors for implementation guidance. Overall, the interviewees provide insights consistent with my empirical analyses.This study makes several contributions to the literature. While prior studies indicate certain prominent standards achieve targeted regulatory objectives, like improving inter-industry revenue comparability (Tillet, 2026), I find that the adoption of standards in general is associated with lower financial reporting quality. Importantly, the evidence suggests that new standards create a distraction effect that lowers financial reporting quality in areas unrelated to the standard being adopted. I also find that client, standard, and auditor-related factors influence the success of implementation. The FASB regularly conducts post-implementation reviews to examine unintended consequences or costs of standards, and these findings provide relevant feedback on the adoption process. This study suggests that one unintended consequence of a new standard is a negative effect on financial reporting quality in the year of adoption.Second, this study introduces a novel AI-based methodology to parse annual reports. Recent research across several streams of literature relies on various methodologies to glean insights from unstructured textual disclosures ranging from basic keyword searches to deep learning neural networks (see Bochkay et al., 2023 for a recent review). While some studies have begun using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) for identification (Bernard et al., 2026), this is the first study using a standard, publicly available LLM model for identification. Furthermore, while many studies examine the effects of accounting standards using financial statement ratios (Khan et al., 2018) or XBRL tags, my approach allows identification of standard adoption for any standard, so long as the impact is disclosed by the firm.Finally, this study contributes to the literature stream on employee workloads. Studies find that human capital resource constraints create higher workloads among employees, which influences disclosure quality (Chen et al., 2023). My study finds that standards likely to require more effort result in lower-quality financial reporting concentrated in the year of adoption. Prior research also investigates factors that increase auditor workload and finds that such increases harm audit quality (Bills et al., 2016; Czerney et al., 2019; Christensen et al., 2021a). This study finds that standards adoption increases auditor workload because auditors assist their clients with implementation, and the ability of an audit office to absorb the increased workload influences their clients’ success in adoption. before.title_zh: 应对新会计准则：对企业及其审计师的影响
before.abstract_zh: 我考察了实施新会计准则对财务报告质量的影响。尽管先前研究表明准则总体上实现了其监管目标，但近期文献发现企业面临显著的技术会计能力约束，这促使我们需要探究会计准则采用对财务报告质量更广泛的影响。我采用一种新颖的基于人工智能的方法来识别受新会计准则影响的企业，发现当企业实施新准则时，财务报告质量下降。证据表明，受损的财务报告质量出现在与新准则无关的会计领域，这与分心效应一致。当企业同时面临其他与会计相关的挑战、会计准则更为复杂以及审计师资源受限时，结果更为显著。这些发现为新会计准则的意外后果提供了证据，并为缓解这些成本的潜在途径提供了启示。

Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors

•
Accounting standards adoption leads to lower financial reporting quality.
•
Adopting firms are 31% more likely to misstate financial statements.
•
The misstatements are observable only in the year of adoption.
•
The misstatements involve areas unrelated to the new accounting standards.
•
Results are more pronounced in resource-constrained firms and auditors.

I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.KeywordsAccounting standards; Financial reporting quality; Audit quality; Resource constraintsJEL classificationM41; M42; M49IntroductionSince the Accounting Standard Codification (ASC) project launched in 2009, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) has issued more than 200 accounting standards updates (ASUs). Most new standards include a section titled “Benefits and Costs,” where the FASB justifies the potential increased cost of financial statement preparation with the additional benefit of improved information quality. Prior research has provided insights about the effects of specific, prominent standards (e.g., Henry et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2019; Tillet, 2026), but there is a paucity of evidence about whether and to what extent FASB standards satisfy the FASB's intent noted in each standard. As prominent standards examined in other studies often involve sweeping changes and are not representative of typical standards, our understanding of the influence of new standards on financial reporting quality is limited. Recent research indicates that firms have limited accounting expertise (Huang et al., 2025) and their behavior toward the typical standard differs from their preparation for prominent standards (e.g., revenue), which suggests that firms may not have available resources to implement new standards. In this study, I examine how new accounting standards affect financial reporting quality and which factors moderate this relationship.Despite more than 15 standards, on average, becoming effective each year, prior studies provide few details about the challenges firms and their auditors face during implementation. Yet, adopting new standards has the potential to affect financial reporting quality for several reasons. Firms often must re-evaluate their existing procedures, implement new IT systems, or hire additional personnel. In addition, adoption increases the workload for both preparers and their auditors, and both groups’ performance declines under such conditions (Chen et al., 2023; Christensen et al., 2021a). Given the ongoing accounting resource strains (AICPA, 2023) and the difficulty investors face when standards change (Dyer et al., 2025), it is important to understand how the implementation of standards influences financial reporting quality.To conduct my empirical analyses, I must identify which firms are affected by new accounting standards. This task is challenging due to varying language and disclosure choices among adopting firms. Prior studies have addressed this challenge by focusing on a single, prominent standard that produced an observable financial statement effect (e.g., Hunsader et al., 2022) or by identifying the types of firms likely affected by a single, new standard (e.g., Khan et al., 2018). As my analysis investigates the effects across all new standards, I develop a new method to identify affected firms. That is, I use a novel AI-based tool to parse more than 50,000 XBRL disclosures and identify firms adopting any standard that materially affects their financial statements. I then examine how standards adoption affects firms’ financial reporting quality.I find that adoption occurs frequently and that it negatively influences the quality of financial reporting. Approximately 37 percent of firm years across my sample are involved in the adoption of a new standard that has a material impact. Moreover, I find that adopting firms are 31 percent more likely to restate their annual filings through an item 4.02 disclosure (Big R restatements) and 44 percent more likely to fail to disclose an existing material weakness than firms unaffected by a new standard. Thus, new standards appear to have an immediate, detrimental effect on financial reporting quality.To better understand how standards adoption harms financial reporting quality, I examine two potential drivers of this effect. First, the firm may face challenges in implementing the standard's requirements, resulting in improper reporting about the subject matter of the standard. With a new standard, firms may not have pertinent expertise or resources to implement the standard without error. Alternatively, firms and their auditors likely recognize the possibility of increased regulatory scrutiny of areas affected by the standard, so they may devote sufficient effort to ensure those areas are reported properly. However, this increased attention may draw resources away from other financial reporting areas, resulting in lower financial reporting quality in areas unaffected by new standards (Kahneman, 1973; Seidel, 2017).To test these competing explanations, I examine the restatement categories associated with standards adoption. I find that the detrimental effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated in accounting areas unrelated to the new standard and completed late in the audit. I corroborate these findings with SEC comment letters. I find that firms adopting new standards are 6.5 percent more likely to receive an SEC comment letter, but I fail to find evidence that these comment letters reference the new standards. Results from these tests suggest that standards adoption diverts firm and auditor attention to the new standard and away from other areas. To corroborate this inference, I examine the duration of this effect. If the impairment stems from a diversion of firm and auditor resources during the adoption, the effect will likely dissipate after the adoption is completed. I find that the reduction in financial reporting quality is evident only in the year of adoption. Collectively, the evidence suggests that the adoption of a new accounting standard is associated with a decrease in financial reporting quality that is concentrated in the adoption year in areas unrelated to the standard itself.I expect that the effect on financial reporting quality differs based on firm, standard, and auditor characteristics, so I next test how these factors influence its magnitude. Regarding firm-level factors, recent research (Huang et al., 2025) suggests that firms often lack sufficient internal accounting expertise to handle increases in workloads that may be required to adopt a standard. I find that financial reporting quality impairments are more pronounced when firms are in unregulated industries, have ongoing mergers, experience accounting personnel turnover, or have existing internal control deficiencies. Collectively, this evidence suggests that concurrent accounting-related challenges influence the effect of adopting new accounting standards.Second, I investigate standard-level factors that may influence the success of adoption. Accounting standards vary in their scope, with some simply modifying minor disclosure requirements while others require significant accounting policy changes. More complex standards are more likely to require additional work from firms and their auditors, which may lead to lower financial reporting quality. I use three proxies for standards complexity: the FOG index, the length of the standard, and the degree to which auditors lobbied for the standard.1 I find that the complexity of the adopted standard exacerbates new standards’ impairment of financial reporting quality.Third, I consider whether auditor-related factors affect the success of the adoption of standards. Auditors can provide assistance to their clients only insofar as they have available resources to increase staffing. Because standards implementation requires additional work, auditors generally attempt to allocate additional employees to affected clients. However, their ability to do so depends on the availability of additional auditors. I expect that offices with more clients concurrently adopting new standards will have fewer available personnel and be less successful in helping clients adopt the latest standards. Consistent with this expectation, I find that the negative effects on financial reporting quality are concentrated among offices that have more clients adopting new standards. I also find that the results are more pronounced for clients of non-Big 4 auditors, which is consistent with Big 4 auditors having more training and support resources, enabling more efficient audit program modifications.Finally, I conduct semi-structured interviews with financial statement preparers and audit partners to provide additional institutional context about how firms and their auditors collaborate to implement new standards.2 Interviewees note that the implementation of new standards requires significant effort and disrupts other processes and that firms often turn to their auditors for implementation guidance. Overall, the interviewees provide insights consistent with my empirical analyses.This study makes several contributions to the literature. While prior studies indicate certain prominent standards achieve targeted regulatory objectives, like improving inter-industry revenue comparability (Tillet, 2026), I find that the adoption of standards in general is associated with lower financial reporting quality. Importantly, the evidence suggests that new standards create a distraction effect that lowers financial reporting quality in areas unrelated to the standard being adopted. I also find that client, standard, and auditor-related factors influence the success of implementation. The FASB regularly conducts post-implementation reviews to examine unintended consequences or costs of standards, and these findings provide relevant feedback on the adoption process. This study suggests that one unintended consequence of a new standard is a negative effect on financial reporting quality in the year of adoption.Second, this study introduces a novel AI-based methodology to parse annual reports. Recent research across several streams of literature relies on various methodologies to glean insights from unstructured textual disclosures ranging from basic keyword searches to deep learning neural networks (see Bochkay et al., 2023 for a recent review). While some studies have begun using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) for identification (Bernard et al., 2026), this is the first study using a standard, publicly available LLM model for identification. Furthermore, while many studies examine the effects of accounting standards using financial statement ratios (Khan et al., 2018) or XBRL tags, my approach allows identification of standard adoption for any standard, so long as the impact is disclosed by the firm.Finally, this study contributes to the literature stream on employee workloads. Studies find that human capital resource constraints create higher workloads among employees, which influences disclosure quality (Chen et al., 2023). My study finds that standards likely to require more effort result in lower-quality financial reporting concentrated in the year of adoption. Prior research also investigates factors that increase auditor workload and finds that such increases harm audit quality (Bills et al., 2016; Czerney et al., 2019; Christensen et al., 2021a). This study finds that standards adoption increases auditor workload because auditors assist their clients with implementation, and the ability of an audit office to absorb the increased workload influences their clients’ success in adoption. Though regulators design new standards to improve disclosure, I find evidence that the adoption of new accounting standards is associated with increased workloads for firms and their auditors, resulting in financial reporting impairments and economically significant costs.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsLiteratureA large body of literature studies the effects of individual accounting standards. existing_records.title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
existing_records.abstract: I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

source_records.title: Measurement error when estimating covenant slack and violations
source_records.abstract: We collect quantitative (true thresholds and realizations) and qualitative (compliance status) covenant information from SEC filings to examine the accuracy of compliance estimates derived using data from commercial databases. Estimated covenant slack frequently overestimates covenant violations, and only rarely understates them, with this asymmetry holding for both qualitative and quantitative disclosers. The non-random structure of this measurement error has implications for research that relies on estimated violations or on precise measurement of covenant realizations near a threshold. Across our two samples of disclosers, we find evidence consistent with the debt covenant hypothesis for debt-to-EBITDA covenants once measurement error is considered. We also show that the lender forbearance rate declines sharply after correcting estimated violations for measurement error, and that true violations, but not estimated violations, are associated with negative stock market reactions and loan renegotiations. Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.

The non-random structure of this measurement error has implications for research that relies on estimated violations or on precise measurement of covenant realizations near a threshold. Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.KeywordsDebt covenants; Covenant slack; Covenant violations; Measurement ErrorJEL classificationG30; M40; M41IntroductionFinancial covenants are ubiquitous in debt contracts and facilitate lending by mitigating conflicts between firms and capital providers (Smith and Warner, 1979; Roberts and Sufi, 2009; Bradley and Roberts, 2015). An important aspect of financial covenant design is the distance between a covenant realization and a covenant threshold, called covenant slack (or tightness), which influences the likelihood of covenant violations. A financial covenant violation occurs when the realization of the contractually defined financial measure, such as debt-to-EBITDA, crosses the covenant threshold specified in the debt contract. An extensive literature, reviewed in Armstrong et al. (2010) and Christensen et al. (2016), examines the determinants and consequences of covenant slack, including covenant violations, and how covenants create incentives for firms to manipulate reported numbers.1Calculating covenant slack requires two data elements: 1) the covenant threshold and 2) the contractually realized covenant amount or ratio (i.e., covenant realization). Researchers typically obtain covenant thresholds from Thomson Reuters’ Dealscan and calculate covenant realizations by applying assumed standardized covenant definitions to Compustat data (e.g., Compustat item OIBDPQ is a proxy for covenant-defined EBITDA). The appropriateness of this approach rests upon the following assumptions. First, covenant thresholds in Dealscan are accurate. Second, covenant types reported by Dealscan are accurate, and the assumed underlying covenant definitions are consistent across firms and contracts. Third, the assumed covenant definitions map accurately to Compustat variables. Violations of these assumptions result in two types of measurement error: threshold measurement error and realization measurement error.Threshold measurement error arises when covenant thresholds from Dealscan (hereafter, estimated thresholds) differ from true covenant thresholds. These differences arise because Dealscan fails to capture planned changes in thresholds over the life of the loan or threshold adjustments from contractual amendments (Roberts, 2015; Li et al., 2016). Realization measurement error arises when covenant realizations derived using Compustat data with assumed covenant definitions (hereafter, estimated realizations) differ from true realizations. This measurement error arises because researchers rely on incorrect covenant definitions, or because covenant-defined measures do not correspond to Compustat variables. For example, financial covenants are commonly defined using non-GAAP numbers that are not available in commercial databases (Leftwich, 1983; Christensen and Nikolaev, 2017). In addition, while researchers rely on standardized definitions (Demerjian and Owens, 2016), covenant definitions for the same covenant type vary widely across debt contracts (Beatty et al., 2019; Badawi et al., 2024).2In this paper, we use a hand-collected dataset of firms’ true covenant realizations and thresholds and covenant compliance status to: (1) investigate and quantify the measurement error associated with traditional measures of covenant slack and covenant violations; (2) identify the source of the measurement error; (3) assess whether using estimated versus true measures of slack or violations yields different inferences; and (4) investigate ways to reduce measurement error.We obtain firms' true covenant realizations and thresholds through the following process. Beginning with 93,092 firm-quarter observations from 2000 to 2016 that can be linked to both Dealscan and Compustat, we manually review a random sample of 1,000 10-K filings to identify whether a firm reports both true covenant thresholds and realizations (i.e., true covenant information) and to examine the language used in these disclosures. We use this information to develop a text-search algorithm that we apply to the Full Sample to identify firms' disclosure of true covenant information. We then hand-collect true covenant information for all covenant types, and focus our attention on the eight most common: interest coverage ratios, fixed charge coverage ratios, debt-to-EBITDA ratios, senior debt-to-EBITDA ratios, current ratios, leverage, net worth, and tangible net worth. This process yields a primary sample of 18,217 unique firm-quarter-covenants corresponding to 9,799 unique firm-quarters (True Slack Sample). To enhance generalizability, we also collect information about firms’ covenant compliance status. Approximately two-thirds of firm-quarter observations in our initial sample (61,303 of 93,092) qualitatively discuss their compliance status with financial covenants (Compliance Sample). Although these disclosures lack true covenant information, they indicate covenant compliance, allowing us to evaluate measurement error in estimated covenant violations in a broader sample than our True Slack Sample.We emphasize that the financial reporting requirements governing disclosure of true thresholds and realizations allow for some managerial discretion, and the True Slack Sample may be confounded by sample selection bias. As such, inferences from the True Slack Sample may not generalize to the broader population of borrowers. The Compliance Sample, which covers about two-thirds of the Full Sample, suffers less from this problem, and supports broader inferences about measurement error in estimated covenant violations, though it does not contain quantitative slack information. Throughout the paper, we report results separately for the Full, Compliance, and True Slack Samples, and interpret True Slack Sample findings cautiously given the concerns related to sample selection.We find that differences between true slack (the distance between true realizations and true thresholds) and estimated slack (the distance between estimated realizations and estimated thresholds) are frequent and meaningful: overall, 82% of the observations display measurement error in covenant slack of at least 10% relative to true slack. Prior research has acknowledged these concerns to some degree by focusing on current ratio covenants (e.g., Dichev and Skinner, 2002; Chava and Roberts, 2008), which are assumed to be less susceptible to measurement error. Our findings suggest that this assumption may not hold more broadly. We document that between 77% (interest coverage and debt-to-EBITDA ratios) and 95% (current ratio) of observations display measurement error of at least 10% relative to true slack. In our data, current ratio covenants display large measurement error at the highest frequency among the covenant types we examine.We also investigate whether the documented measurement error arises primarily from realization measurement error, threshold measurement error, or both. We show that realization measurement error is the primary source of the problem. This is important because while threshold measurement error can largely be addressed by collecting true thresholds from loan contracts and their amendments, which are filed with the SEC, realization error is more difficult to resolve. Consequently, estimated slack may still suffer from considerable measurement error even when researchers hand-collect data on thresholds (i.e., true thresholds) but continue to rely on estimated realizations (e.g., Chava and Roberts, 2008; Bordeman and Demerjian, 2022). We further show that large measurement error in slack, thresholds, and realizations vary predictably with firm and loan contract characteristics.Next, we examine whether this measurement error affects the identification of covenant violations. At the firm-quarter level, relying on estimated slack substantially overstates the number of covenant violations, with nearly 96 of every 100 estimated violations being Type I Errors (i.e., estimated slack identifies a violation while true slack does not). Our Compliance Sample, which offers more generalizable evidence, indicates similar severity: 95 of every 100 estimated violations are Type I Errors. In both samples, measurement error in estimated slack is asymmetric: Type I Errors are common, while Type II Errors (i.e., true slack identifies a violation while estimated slack does not) are rare.The presence of frequent, non-standard measurement error raises the possibility that inferences in covenant research that relies on estimated slack may be sensitive to this error. We assess this possibility by revisiting four major streams of the debt literature. These streams differ in how covenant slack or violations are used (whether as explanatory variables, dependent variables, or forcing variables in causal designs) and in whether valid inference requires precise distance from covenant thresholds or only an ordinal ranking of slack. By revisiting these studies, we assess when measurement error likely affects inference and when findings based on commonly used approaches remain reliable.We start with research requiring precise measurement of covenant slack, including studies testing the debt covenant hypothesis (DCH) (Watts and Zimmerman, 1978). Dichev and Skinner (2002) document bunching around covenant thresholds for current ratio and net worth covenants, consistent with the DCH. Bordeman and Demerjian (2022) extend this evidence using more recent data and additional covenant types, documenting bunching for current ratio and net worth but not for debt-to-EBITDA covenants. These studies rely on estimated slack as a proxy for true slack. We provide two pieces of evidence on whether measurement error affects inferences about the DCH. First, within our True Slack Sample, which covers approximately ten percent of the Full Sample, the distribution of true slack around the debt-to-EBITDA threshold displays a sharp discontinuity that is absent when slack is measured with error. Second, within our Compliance Sample, which covers approximately two-thirds of the Full Sample, we find a one-sided concentration of Type I errors in the bins immediately to the left of the threshold. These observations are incorrectly classified as violations (slack < 0) when in fact they belong in the non-violation region (slack ≥ 0). Under any reasonable assumption about where those misclassified observations sit within the non-violation region, the resulting distribution displays a sharp and large discontinuity around the threshold, consistent with the DCH. Thus, our data suggest that measurement error obscures the magnitude and pervasiveness of the DCH.We next reexamine emerging evidence on lender forbearance. We replicate the central findings of Bird et al. (2022a, 2022b) that lenders do not enforce most violations and that enforcement varies with lenders’ short-term incentives using estimated slack. We then examine the sensitivity of these findings to measurement error using our True Slack and Compliance samples. While Bird et al. (2022a) conclude that lenders do not enforce 9 out of 10 violations, we find that approximately 9 out of 10 of all true violations are enforced once Type I errors are corrected. Our analyses suggest the difference between our findings and those of Bird et al. (2022a) is consistent with Type I errors in estimated violations, and is observed in both our True Slack and Compliance Samples. Similarly, we successfully replicate the finding in Bird et al. (2022b) that lenders are more likely to enforce violations when facing short-term earnings incentives in both our True Slack and Compliance Samples, but find it is not statistically detectable in those samples once measurement error is reduced. These two replications illustrate that measurement error can bias estimated coefficients toward zero (attenuation bias) or away from zero (spurious correlations) depending on the setting. Consequently, researchers should not assume their estimates are always a lower bound of the true effect.One insight emerging from our reexaminations of lender forbearance is that measurement errors in estimated covenant violations can introduce severe attenuation bias that may impair researchers’ ability to find empirical support for otherwise sound economic relations. Consistent with this possibility, we reveal two insights that would be concealed by measurement error in estimated slack: while estimated violations are not associated with negative stock market reactions or a higher likelihood of future loan renegotiation, true covenant violations are.Next, we revisit research that uses covenant slack as a dependent variable, focusing on studies that examine the determinants of initial covenant slack (or tightness), including borrower characteristics (Demiroglu and James, 2010; Rauh and Sufi, 2010), lender characteristics (Murfin, 2012), and the relationship between the two (Prilmeier, 2017). To explore whether measurement error affects this research, we reexamine Prilmeier's (2017) finding that lender relationships and firm risk explain variation in covenant tightness. We find that when we replace estimated slack with true slack, not only are the findings robust; they become economically and statistically stronger. Collectively, our evidence suggests that research on the determinants of covenant slack is less susceptible to measurement error concerns, likely because covenant slack appears as the dependent variable and estimated and true slack display a positive, relatively high correlation.Finally, we revisit the regression discontinuity (RD) approach introduced by Chava and Roberts (2008) to estimate the causal effects of covenant violations. Valid inference using this design requires that the running variable, covenant slack, is not manipulated around the threshold. We show that measurement error in estimated slack masks evidence of threshold manipulation that is present in true slack: formal manipulation tests following Cattaneo et al. (2018) indicate a smooth density when applied to estimated slack but reveal manipulation when applied to true slack. This manipulation invalidates the design, and is consistent with the bunching documented in Dichev and Skinner (2002) and with our reexamination of the DCH. We then consider how researchers might test hypotheses about the consequences of covenant violations once manipulation is known to be present. Neither donut designs nor the bounds of Gerard et al. (2020) perform well in this setting, the former because measurement error prevents reliably identifying observations near the threshold, and the latter because it presumes an accurately measured running variable and yields wide bounds given the extent of bunching we document in true slack. Collectively, these findings should caution researchers about using RDDs with estimated covenant slack to draw causal inference about the consequences of covenant violations.Overall, our replications convey four messages driven by the unreliability of estimated slack as a measure for true slack. First, for research questions requiring precise measurement of covenant slack, inferences are likely to be sharper when true covenant information is available. Second, for research that focuses on identifying covenant violations, measurement error in estimated slack can bias estimates in either direction, and these concerns can be mitigated by using firm compliance disclosures. Third, for research that seeks to explain variation in covenant slack, measurement error is less problematic because estimated and true slack are highly correlated, and the ordinal ranking of slack contains less error. Finally, researchers should interpret evidence from RDDs around covenant violations cautiously given the limits of estimated slack as a proxy for true slack and the threshold manipulation we document in true slack.We conclude by exploring practical approaches to mitigate the consequences of measurement error. First, we examine whether researchers could hand-collect covenant definitions from loan contracts and accurately calculate realizations based on these definitions using information from SEC filings. Our investigation using a hand-collected sample of contractual definitions of EBITDA-based covenants suggests a broadly applicable solution that eliminates measurement error is unlikely. Contractual EBITDA definitions frequently include non-standard adjustments, such as other non-cash items, which are not reported in financial statements (or in Compustat), and firms often disclose insufficient detail in their financial statement notes to determine these adjustment amounts. We also assess whether adjusting for compensation-related expenses or restricting the sample to contracts with precise, simplified definitions reduces measurement error in EBITDA-based covenants. Both approaches yield improvements, with the latter producing the greatest gains, at the cost of sample attrition. Together, these findings highlight both the progress researchers can make in reducing measurement error and the inherent challenges that remain.Our study is subject to limitations. While firms are likely to follow SEC guidance about discussions concerning debt covenants (Deloitte, 2017; EY, 2017), they retain some discretion in disclosing this information. We find that disclosing firms are larger, more leveraged, and closer to default than non-disclosing firms, and disclosure choices are highly persistent over time. As a consequence, the distribution of true slack and rate of true violations in the True Slack Sample, which covers roughly ten percent of the Full Sample, may not match those of non-disclosing firms. Moreover, the True Slack Sample is smaller than those used in many existing studies. We take numerous steps to address this concern, such as replicating findings in our True Slack sample with estimated slack, and generally find results that suggest sample selection bias is not the driving force behind our conclusions. Nonetheless, we cannot entirely rule out the possibility. The Compliance Sample, which covers about two-thirds of the Full Sample, supports broader inferences about measurement error in estimated violations but cannot speak to the distribution of slack. We therefore interpret findings from the True Slack Sample and Compliance Sample as evidence about a specific, economically meaningful subsample of borrowers rather than the universe of borrowers, and acknowledge that our results may not generalize to firms that do not disclose information about covenant compliance.With these limitations in mind, our study makes several contributions. Although prior research acknowledges potential measurement issues associated with estimated covenant slack (Dichev and Skinner, 2002; Chava and Roberts, 2008; Demerjian and Owens, 2016), we are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to document that this measurement error is frequent and large, and extends to all common covenant types. This insight is relevant for both academic research and practice, including the FASB's ongoing project on key performance indicators.3Our second contribution is to the growing literature exploring research design issues that may bias inferences (Atanasov and Black, 2016; Donelson et al., 2022; Jennings et al., 2024; Breuer and DeHaan, 2024). We identify situations where measurement error issues may create large biases and where these issues may be less problematic. We show that measurement error in estimated slack is problematic for research requiring precise identification of the distance between covenant realization and covenant thresholds. We base these conclusions on three grounds: (1) estimated slack does not allow researchers to precisely measure true slack, making it nearly impossible to study intervals near the threshold; (2) measurement error in estimated covenant slack is not “white noise”, namely, it is not symmetrically distributed around zero; and (3) measurement error in estimated covenant slack covaries predictably with firm and contract characteristics. proposed.title: Measurement error when estimating covenant slack and violations
proposed.abstract: We collect quantitative (true thresholds and realizations) and qualitative (compliance status) covenant information from SEC filings to examine the accuracy of compliance estimates derived using data from commercial databases. Estimated covenant slack frequently overestimates covenant violations, and only rarely understates them, with this asymmetry holding for both qualitative and quantitative disclosers. The non-random structure of this measurement error has implications for research that relies on estimated violations or on precise measurement of covenant realizations near a threshold. Across our two samples of disclosers, we find evidence consistent with the debt covenant hypothesis for debt-to-EBITDA covenants once measurement error is considered. We also show that the lender forbearance rate declines sharply after correcting estimated violations for measurement error, and that true violations, but not estimated violations, are associated with negative stock market reactions and loan renegotiations. Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.

before.title_zh: 估计契约松弛与违约时的测量误差
before.abstract_zh: 我们从SEC文件中收集定量的（真实阈值和实现值）和定性的（合规状态）契约信息，以检验使用商业数据库数据得出的合规估计的准确性。估计的契约松弛经常高估契约违约，而很少低估违约，这种不对称性在定性披露者和定量披露者中都成立。这种测量误差的非随机结构对依赖估计违约或依赖对阈值附近契约实现值进行精确测量的研究具有启示意义。在我们的两个披露者样本中，一旦考虑测量误差，我们发现与债务契约假说一致的证据，针对债务与EBITDA契约。我们还表明，在将估计违约针对测量误差进行校正后，贷款人宽限率急剧下降，并且真实违约——而非估计违约——与负面的股票市场反应和贷款重新谈判相关。最后，我们探讨减少测量误差的实用方法。
