Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.KeywordsDebt covenants; Covenant slack; Covenant violations; Measurement ErrorJEL classificationG30; M40; M41IntroductionFinancial covenants are ubiquitous in debt contracts and facilitate lending by mitigating conflicts between firms and capital providers (Smith and Warner, 1979; Roberts and Sufi, 2009; Bradley and Roberts, 2015). An important aspect of financial covenant design is the distance between a covenant realization and a covenant threshold, called covenant slack (or tightness), which influences the likelihood of covenant violations. A financial covenant violation occurs when the realization of the contractually defined financial measure, such as debt-to-EBITDA, crosses the covenant threshold specified in the debt contract. An extensive literature, reviewed in Armstrong et al. (2010) and Christensen et al. (2016), examines the determinants and consequences of covenant slack, including covenant violations, and how covenants create incentives for firms to manipulate reported numbers.1Calculating covenant slack requires two data elements: 1) the covenant threshold and 2) the contractually realized covenant amount or ratio (i.e., covenant realization). Researchers typically obtain covenant thresholds from Thomson Reuters’ Dealscan and calculate covenant realizations by applying assumed standardized covenant definitions to Compustat data (e.g., Compustat item OIBDPQ is a proxy for covenant-defined EBITDA). The appropriateness of this approach rests upon the following assumptions. First, covenant thresholds in Dealscan are accurate. Second, covenant types reported by Dealscan are accurate, and the assumed underlying covenant definitions are consistent across firms and contracts. Third, the assumed covenant definitions map accurately to Compustat variables. Violations of these assumptions result in two types of measurement error: threshold measurement error and realization measurement error.Threshold measurement error arises when covenant thresholds from Dealscan (hereafter, estimated thresholds) differ from true covenant thresholds. These differences arise because Dealscan fails to capture planned changes in thresholds over the life of the loan or threshold adjustments from contractual amendments (Roberts, 2015; Li et al., 2016). Realization measurement error arises when covenant realizations derived using Compustat data with assumed covenant definitions (hereafter, estimated realizations) differ from true realizations. This measurement error arises because researchers rely on incorrect covenant definitions, or because covenant-defined measures do not correspond to Compustat variables. For example, financial covenants are commonly defined using non-GAAP numbers that are not available in commercial databases (Leftwich, 1983; Christensen and Nikolaev, 2017). In addition, while researchers rely on standardized definitions (Demerjian and Owens, 2016), covenant definitions for the same covenant type vary widely across debt contracts (Beatty et al., 2019; Badawi et al., 2024).2In this paper, we use a hand-collected dataset of firms’ true covenant realizations and thresholds and covenant compliance status to: (1) investigate and quantify the measurement error associated with traditional measures of covenant slack and covenant violations; (2) identify the source of the measurement error; (3) assess whether using estimated versus true measures of slack or violations yields different inferences; and (4) investigate ways to reduce measurement error.We obtain firms' true covenant realizations and thresholds through the following process. Beginning with 93,092 firm-quarter observations from 2000 to 2016 that can be linked to both Dealscan and Compustat, we manually review a random sample of 1,000 10-K filings to identify whether a firm reports both true covenant thresholds and realizations (i.e., true covenant information) and to examine the language used in these disclosures. We use this information to develop a text-search algorithm that we apply to the Full Sample to identify firms' disclosure of true covenant information. We then hand-collect true covenant information for all covenant types, and focus our attention on the eight most common: interest coverage ratios, fixed charge coverage ratios, debt-to-EBITDA ratios, senior debt-to-EBITDA ratios, current ratios, leverage, net worth, and tangible net worth. This process yields a primary sample of 18,217 unique firm-quarter-covenants corresponding to 9,799 unique firm-quarters (True Slack Sample). To enhance generalizability, we also collect information about firms’ covenant compliance status. Approximately two-thirds of firm-quarter observations in our initial sample (61,303 of 93,092) qualitatively discuss their compliance status with financial covenants (Compliance Sample). Although these disclosures lack true covenant information, they indicate covenant compliance, allowing us to evaluate measurement error in estimated covenant violations in a broader sample than our True Slack Sample.We emphasize that the financial reporting requirements governing disclosure of true thresholds and realizations allow for some managerial discretion, and the True Slack Sample may be confounded by sample selection bias. As such, inferences from the True Slack Sample may not generalize to the broader population of borrowers. The Compliance Sample, which covers about two-thirds of the Full Sample, suffers less from this problem, and supports broader inferences about measurement error in estimated covenant violations, though it does not contain quantitative slack information. Throughout the paper, we report results separately for the Full, Compliance, and True Slack Samples, and interpret True Slack Sample findings cautiously given the concerns related to sample selection.We find that differences between true slack (the distance between true realizations and true thresholds) and estimated slack (the distance between estimated realizations and estimated thresholds) are frequent and meaningful: overall, 82% of the observations display measurement error in covenant slack of at least 10% relative to true slack. Prior research has acknowledged these concerns to some degree by focusing on current ratio covenants (e.g., Dichev and Skinner, 2002; Chava and Roberts, 2008), which are assumed to be less susceptible to measurement error. Our findings suggest that this assumption may not hold more broadly. We document that between 77% (interest coverage and debt-to-EBITDA ratios) and 95% (current ratio) of observations display measurement error of at least 10% relative to true slack. In our data, current ratio covenants display large measurement error at the highest frequency among the covenant types we examine.We also investigate whether the documented measurement error arises primarily from realization measurement error, threshold measurement error, or both. We show that realization measurement error is the primary source of the problem. This is important because while threshold measurement error can largely be addressed by collecting true thresholds from loan contracts and their amendments, which are filed with the SEC, realization error is more difficult to resolve. Consequently, estimated slack may still suffer from considerable measurement error even when researchers hand-collect data on thresholds (i.e., true thresholds) but continue to rely on estimated realizations (e.g., Chava and Roberts, 2008; Bordeman and Demerjian, 2022). We further show that large measurement error in slack, thresholds, and realizations vary predictably with firm and loan contract characteristics.Next, we examine whether this measurement error affects the identification of covenant violations. At the firm-quarter level, relying on estimated slack substantially overstates the number of covenant violations, with nearly 96 of every 100 estimated violations being Type I Errors (i.e., estimated slack identifies a violation while true slack does not). Our Compliance Sample, which offers more generalizable evidence, indicates similar severity: 95 of every 100 estimated violations are Type I Errors. In both samples, measurement error in estimated slack is asymmetric: Type I Errors are common, while Type II Errors (i.e., true slack identifies a violation while estimated slack does not) are rare.The presence of frequent, non-standard measurement error raises the possibility that inferences in covenant research that relies on estimated slack may be sensitive to this error. We assess this possibility by revisiting four major streams of the debt literature. These streams differ in how covenant slack or violations are used (whether as explanatory variables, dependent variables, or forcing variables in causal designs) and in whether valid inference requires precise distance from covenant thresholds or only an ordinal ranking of slack. By revisiting these studies, we assess when measurement error likely affects inference and when findings based on commonly used approaches remain reliable.We start with research requiring precise measurement of covenant slack, including studies testing the debt covenant hypothesis (DCH) (Watts and Zimmerman, 1978). Dichev and Skinner (2002) document bunching around covenant thresholds for current ratio and net worth covenants, consistent with the DCH. Bordeman and Demerjian (2022) extend this evidence using more recent data and additional covenant types, documenting bunching for current ratio and net worth but not for debt-to-EBITDA covenants. These studies rely on estimated slack as a proxy for true slack. We provide two pieces of evidence on whether measurement error affects inferences about the DCH. First, within our True Slack Sample, which covers approximately ten percent of the Full Sample, the distribution of true slack around the debt-to-EBITDA threshold displays a sharp discontinuity that is absent when slack is measured with error. Second, within our Compliance Sample, which covers approximately two-thirds of the Full Sample, we find a one-sided concentration of Type I errors in the bins immediately to the left of the threshold. These observations are incorrectly classified as violations (slack < 0) when in fact they belong in the non-violation region (slack ≥ 0). Under any reasonable assumption about where those misclassified observations sit within the non-violation region, the resulting distribution displays a sharp and large discontinuity around the threshold, consistent with the DCH. Thus, our data suggest that measurement error obscures the magnitude and pervasiveness of the DCH.We next reexamine emerging evidence on lender forbearance. We replicate the central findings of Bird et al. (2022a, 2022b) that lenders do not enforce most violations and that enforcement varies with lenders’ short-term incentives using estimated slack. We then examine the sensitivity of these findings to measurement error using our True Slack and Compliance samples. While Bird et al. (2022a) conclude that lenders do not enforce 9 out of 10 violations, we find that approximately 9 out of 10 of all true violations are enforced once Type I errors are corrected. Our analyses suggest the difference between our findings and those of Bird et al. (2022a) is consistent with Type I errors in estimated violations, and is observed in both our True Slack and Compliance Samples. Similarly, we successfully replicate the finding in Bird et al. (2022b) that lenders are more likely to enforce violations when facing short-term earnings incentives in both our True Slack and Compliance Samples, but find it is not statistically detectable in those samples once measurement error is reduced. These two replications illustrate that measurement error can bias estimated coefficients toward zero (attenuation bias) or away from zero (spurious correlations) depending on the setting. Consequently, researchers should not assume their estimates are always a lower bound of the true effect.One insight emerging from our reexaminations of lender forbearance is that measurement errors in estimated covenant violations can introduce severe attenuation bias that may impair researchers’ ability to find empirical support for otherwise sound economic relations. Consistent with this possibility, we reveal two insights that would be concealed by measurement error in estimated slack: while estimated violations are not associated with negative stock market reactions or a higher likelihood of future loan renegotiation, true covenant violations are.Next, we revisit research that uses covenant slack as a dependent variable, focusing on studies that examine the determinants of initial covenant slack (or tightness), including borrower characteristics (Demiroglu and James, 2010; Rauh and Sufi, 2010), lender characteristics (Murfin, 2012), and the relationship between the two (Prilmeier, 2017). To explore whether measurement error affects this research, we reexamine Prilmeier's (2017) finding that lender relationships and firm risk explain variation in covenant tightness. We find that when we replace estimated slack with true slack, not only are the findings robust; they become economically and statistically stronger. Collectively, our evidence suggests that research on the determinants of covenant slack is less susceptible to measurement error concerns, likely because covenant slack appears as the dependent variable and estimated and true slack display a positive, relatively high correlation.Finally, we revisit the regression discontinuity (RD) approach introduced by Chava and Roberts (2008) to estimate the causal effects of covenant violations. Valid inference using this design requires that the running variable, covenant slack, is not manipulated around the threshold. We show that measurement error in estimated slack masks evidence of threshold manipulation that is present in true slack: formal manipulation tests following Cattaneo et al. (2018) indicate a smooth density when applied to estimated slack but reveal manipulation when applied to true slack. This manipulation invalidates the design, and is consistent with the bunching documented in Dichev and Skinner (2002) and with our reexamination of the DCH. We then consider how researchers might test hypotheses about the consequences of covenant violations once manipulation is known to be present. Neither donut designs nor the bounds of Gerard et al. (2020) perform well in this setting, the former because measurement error prevents reliably identifying observations near the threshold, and the latter because it presumes an accurately measured running variable and yields wide bounds given the extent of bunching we document in true slack. Collectively, these findings should caution researchers about using RDDs with estimated covenant slack to draw causal inference about the consequences of covenant violations.Overall, our replications convey four messages driven by the unreliability of estimated slack as a measure for true slack. First, for research questions requiring precise measurement of covenant slack, inferences are likely to be sharper when true covenant information is available. Second, for research that focuses on identifying covenant violations, measurement error in estimated slack can bias estimates in either direction, and these concerns can be mitigated by using firm compliance disclosures. Third, for research that seeks to explain variation in covenant slack, measurement error is less problematic because estimated and true slack are highly correlated, and the ordinal ranking of slack contains less error. Finally, researchers should interpret evidence from RDDs around covenant violations cautiously given the limits of estimated slack as a proxy for true slack and the threshold manipulation we document in true slack.We conclude by exploring practical approaches to mitigate the consequences of measurement error. First, we examine whether researchers could hand-collect covenant definitions from loan contracts and accurately calculate realizations based on these definitions using information from SEC filings. Our investigation using a hand-collected sample of contractual definitions of EBITDA-based covenants suggests a broadly applicable solution that eliminates measurement error is unlikely. Contractual EBITDA definitions frequently include non-standard adjustments, such as other non-cash items, which are not reported in financial statements (or in Compustat), and firms often disclose insufficient detail in their financial statement notes to determine these adjustment amounts. We also assess whether adjusting for compensation-related expenses or restricting the sample to contracts with precise, simplified definitions reduces measurement error in EBITDA-based covenants. Both approaches yield improvements, with the latter producing the greatest gains, at the cost of sample attrition. Together, these findings highlight both the progress researchers can make in reducing measurement error and the inherent challenges that remain.Our study is subject to limitations. While firms are likely to follow SEC guidance about discussions concerning debt covenants (Deloitte, 2017; EY, 2017), they retain some discretion in disclosing this information. We find that disclosing firms are larger, more leveraged, and closer to default than non-disclosing firms, and disclosure choices are highly persistent over time. As a consequence, the distribution of true slack and rate of true violations in the True Slack Sample, which covers roughly ten percent of the Full Sample, may not match those of non-disclosing firms. Moreover, the True Slack Sample is smaller than those used in many existing studies. We take numerous steps to address this concern, such as replicating findings in our True Slack sample with estimated slack, and generally find results that suggest sample selection bias is not the driving force behind our conclusions. Nonetheless, we cannot entirely rule out the possibility. The Compliance Sample, which covers about two-thirds of the Full Sample, supports broader inferences about measurement error in estimated violations but cannot speak to the distribution of slack. We therefore interpret findings from the True Slack Sample and Compliance Sample as evidence about a specific, economically meaningful subsample of borrowers rather than the universe of borrowers, and acknowledge that our results may not generalize to firms that do not disclose information about covenant compliance.With these limitations in mind, our study makes several contributions. Although prior research acknowledges potential measurement issues associated with estimated covenant slack (Dichev and Skinner, 2002; Chava and Roberts, 2008; Demerjian and Owens, 2016), we are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to document that this measurement error is frequent and large, and extends to all common covenant types. We further characterize the nature of this measurement error by showing that it predominantly results in the overstatement of covenant violations (Type I error) and only rarely in their understatement (Type II error), implying that the measurement error is not random. This insight is relevant for both academic research and practice, including the FASB's ongoing project on key performance indicators.3Our second contribution is to the growing literature exploring research design issues that may bias inferences (Atanasov and Black, 2016; Donelson et al., 2022; Jennings et al., 2024; Breuer and DeHaan, 2024). We identify situations where measurement error issues may create large biases and where these issues may be less problematic. We show that measurement error in estimated slack is problematic for research requiring precise identification of the distance between covenant realization and covenant thresholds. We base these conclusions on three grounds: (1) estimated slack does not allow researchers to precisely measure true slack, making it nearly impossible to study intervals near the threshold; (2) measurement error in estimated covenant slack is not “white noise”, namely, it is not symmetrically distributed around zero; and (3) measurement error in estimated covenant slack covaries predictably with firm and contract characteristics. Thus, we invite researchers to exercise care when using estimated covenant slack as an explanatory variable, particularly when using it to identify observations precisely located around covenant thresholds. At the same time, measurement error appears less problematic for research on the relative magnitude of slack, such as papers on the determinants of covenant tightness.Lastly, we offer researchers some solutions to these measurement error issues, with the caveat that considerable measurement error remains. We also plan to make our two new databases available. Researchers can use the first database, which reports firms’ qualitative disclosures about their compliance status with covenants, to remove many Type I errors in estimated covenant violations. Researchers can use the second database, which reports true covenant realizations and thresholds, to completely remove measurement error in covenant slack, at the cost of a smaller, arguably selected sample. At a minimum, we encourage researchers to use this sample to gauge the significance of measurement error problems in their study (for instance, by correlating their variable(s) of interest and measurement error in covenant slack).Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsData collectionWe need information on both true covenant thresholds and realizations to analyze measurement error when estimating covenant slack and covenant violations. proposed.title: Measurement error when estimating covenant slack and violations
proposed.abstract: We collect quantitative (true thresholds and realizations) and qualitative (compliance status) covenant information from SEC filings to examine the accuracy of compliance estimates derived using data from commercial databases. Estimated covenant slack frequently overestimates covenant violations, and only rarely understates them, with this asymmetry holding for both qualitative and quantitative disclosers. The non-random structure of this measurement error has implications for research that relies on estimated violations or on precise measurement of covenant realizations near a threshold. Across our two samples of disclosers, we find evidence consistent with the debt covenant hypothesis for debt-to-EBITDA covenants once measurement error is considered. We also show that the lender forbearance rate declines sharply after correcting estimated violations for measurement error, and that true violations, but not estimated violations, are associated with negative stock market reactions and loan renegotiations. Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.

after.abstract_zh: 我们从SEC文件中收集定量的（真实阈值和实现值）和定性的（合规状态）契约信息，以检验使用商业数据库数据得出的合规估计的准确性。估计的契约松弛经常高估契约违约，而很少低估违约，这种不对称性在定性披露者和定量披露者中都成立。这种测量误差的非随机结构对依赖估计违约或依赖对阈值附近契约实现值进行精确测量的研究具有启示意义。在我们的两个披露者样本中，一旦考虑测量误差，我们发现与债务契约假说一致的证据，针对债务与EBITDA契约。我们还表明，在将估计违约针对测量误差进行校正后，贷款人宽限率急剧下降，并且真实违约——而非估计违约——与负面的股票市场反应和贷款重新谈判相关。最后，我们探讨减少测量误差的实用方法。

existing_records.title: Measurement error when estimating covenant slack and violations

authors.name: Scott Dyreng, Elia Ferracuti, Robert Hills, Matthew Kubic

existing_records.abstract: We collect quantitative (true thresholds and realizations) and qualitative (compliance status) covenant information from SEC filings to examine the accuracy of compliance estimates derived using data from commercial databases. Estimated covenant slack frequently overestimates covenant violations, and only rarely understates them, with this asymmetry holding for both qualitative and quantitative disclosers. The non-random structure of this measurement error has implications for research that relies on estimated violations or on precise measurement of covenant realizations near a threshold. Across our two samples of disclosers, we find evidence consistent with the debt covenant hypothesis for debt-to-EBITDA covenants once measurement error is considered. We also show that the lender forbearance rate declines sharply after correcting estimated violations for measurement error, and that true violations, but not estimated violations, are associated with negative stock market reactions and loan renegotiations. Finally, we investigate practical approaches to reduce measurement error.

source_records.title: Regulating via social media: Deterrence effects of the SEC's use of Twitter
source_records.abstract: This paper presents the ﬁrst evidence of the eﬀect of ﬁnancial regulators’ social media use on corporate and individual behavior. Using the staggered launch of U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regional oﬃces’ Twitter accounts, I ﬁnd that ﬁnancial regulators’ presence on social media reduces opportunistic insider trading, customer complaints against investment advisers, and ﬁnancial misrepor ting. Additional tests suggest that the salience and dissemination of regional oﬃces’ enforcement activities via Twitter play a role. The deterrence eﬀect of SEC regional oﬃces’ Twitter use is concentrated among oﬃces with more followers, ﬁrms with more retail investors, and advisers with more retail clients. I also show that investors react more strongly to enforcement actions after the enforced ﬁrm’s regional oﬃce initiates Twitter use. Taken together, the results suggest that ﬁnancial regulators’ use of social media helps deter misconduct. Lin

before.title_zh: 通过社交媒体进行监管：美国证券交易委员会使用Twitter的威慑效应
before.abstract_zh: 本文首次提供了金融监管机构使用社交媒体对公司和个人行为影响的证据。利用美国证券交易委员会（SEC）各地区办公室Twitter账户的分批推出，我发现金融监管机构在社交媒体上的存在减少了机会主义内幕交易、针对投资顾问的客户投诉以及财务错报。额外测试表明，地区办公室通过Twitter发布执法活动的显著性和传播发挥了作用。SEC地区办公室使用Twitter的威慑效应集中在拥有更多关注者的办公室、拥有更多散户投资者的公司以及拥有更多散户客户的投资顾问中。我还表明，在被执法公司的地区办公室开始使用Twitter后，投资者对执法行动的反应更强烈。总体而言，结果表明金融监管机构使用社交媒体有助于遏制不当行为。Lin

existing_records.title: Regulating via social media: Deterrence effects of the SEC's use of Twitter

authors.name: Raphael Duguay, Jinjie Lin, Jake Thomas, Laiyi Yin

existing_records.abstract: This paper presents the ﬁrst evidence of the eﬀect of ﬁnancial regulators’ social media use on corporate and individual behavior. Using the staggered launch of U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regional oﬃces’ Twitter accounts, I ﬁnd that ﬁnancial regulators’ presence on social media reduces opportunistic insider trading, customer complaints against investment advisers, and ﬁnancial misrepor ting. Additional tests suggest that the salience and dissemination of regional oﬃces’ enforcement activities via Twitter play a role. The deterrence eﬀect of SEC regional oﬃces’ Twitter use is concentrated among oﬃces with more followers, ﬁrms with more retail investors, and advisers with more retail clients. I also show that investors react more strongly to enforcement actions after the enforced ﬁrm’s regional oﬃce initiates Twitter use. Taken together, the results suggest that ﬁnancial regulators’ use of social media helps deter misconduct. Lin

after.title_zh: 通过社交媒体进行监管：美国证券交易委员会使用Twitter的威慑效应
after.abstract_zh: 本文首次提供了金融监管机构使用社交媒体对公司和个人行为影响的证据。利用美国证券交易委员会（SEC）各地区办公室Twitter账户的分批推出，我发现金融监管机构在社交媒体上的存在减少了机会主义内幕交易、针对投资顾问的客户投诉以及财务错报。额外测试表明，地区办公室通过Twitter发布执法活动的显著性和传播发挥了作用。SEC地区办公室使用Twitter的威慑效应集中在拥有更多关注者的办公室、拥有更多散户投资者的公司以及拥有更多散户客户的投资顾问中。我还表明，在被执法公司的地区办公室开始使用Twitter后，投资者对执法行动的反应更强烈。总体而言，结果表明金融监管机构使用社交媒体有助于遏制不当行为。Lin

source_records.abstract: Bhojraj et al. (2026) provide novel evidence that systemically large banks' internal loan loss forecasts systematically overreact to new information and that this overreaction is economically meaningful for loan loss provisioning. Our discussion focuses on whether the evidence identifies representativeness bias, as opposed to a broader set of behavioral, institutional, and economic mechanisms. We argue that the paper more convincingly documents overreaction than it isolates representativeness as the underlying mechanism. We revisit the role of bank information environment, data generating process, COVID-era uncertainty, endogenous bank responses, regulatory influences, and the interpretation of the CECL (Current Expected Credit Losses) results relative to subsidiaries of IFRS 9 adopters. While several additional analyses are supportive of biased expectations, others suggest a more cautious reading of the mechanism. Our overall takeaway is that the paper's central contribution would be strengthened by framing the evidence more directly around overreaction in bank expectations formation and its implications for provisioning, while leaving greater room for multiple coexisting mechanisms and future research on how behavioral forces enter bank forecasting environments.

existing_records.title: Imperfect expectations in loan loss forecasts
existing_records.abstract: Forecasts of future realized loan losses that deviate from rational expectations can impact banks' loan loss provisions, lending procyclicality, and financial stability, especially under the forward-looking current expected credit losses (CECL) model. The behavioral finance literature suggests that bank forecasts are influenced by the representativeness heuristic, which posits that, in forming estimates of future events, forecasters overreact to current circumstances. Leveraging confidential supervisory data from FR Y-14A filings, we document the presence of such overreaction in banks' forecasts of net loan charge-offs. We find that revisions of these forecasts (current forecast minus previous forecast) are negatively associated with the corresponding forecast errors (realized minus current forecast), and this pattern strengthens for longer-horizon forecasts. Successive forecasts of the same future net loan charge-offs exhibit negatively autocorrelated revisions and gradually converge to the realization, indicating the continued presence and gradual resolution of overreaction over time. The overreaction affects loan loss provision in the same direction as the forecast bias, especially for CECL adopters. This effect of overreaction under CECL is more pronounced for longer-horizon forecasts and banks with longer-maturity loans. Supporting the prevalence of this bias, we observe overreaction in banks’ forecasts across loan types and of regional macroeconomic conditions.

existing_records.abstract: Bhojraj et al. (2026) provide novel evidence that systemically large banks' internal loan loss forecasts systematically overreact to new information and that this overreaction is economically meaningful for loan loss provisioning. Our discussion focuses on whether the evidence identifies representativeness bias, as opposed to a broader set of behavioral, institutional, and economic mechanisms. We argue that the paper more convincingly documents overreaction than it isolates representativeness as the underlying mechanism. We revisit the role of bank information environment, data generating process, COVID-era uncertainty, endogenous bank responses, regulatory influences, and the interpretation of the CECL (Current Expected Credit Losses) results relative to subsidiaries of IFRS 9 adopters. While several additional analyses are supportive of biased expectations, others suggest a more cautious reading of the mechanism. Our overall takeaway is that the paper's central contribution would be strengthened by framing the evidence more directly around overreaction in bank expectations formation and its implications for provisioning, while leaving greater room for multiple coexisting mechanisms and future research on how behavioral forces enter bank forecasting environments.

before.abstract_zh: Bhojraj等（2026）提供了新颖的证据，表明系统重要性大型银行的内部贷款损失预测会系统性地对新信息过度反应，且这种过度反应对贷款损失拨备具有经济意义上的重要性。我们的讨论聚焦于这些证据是否识别出了代表性偏差，而非更广泛的行为、制度与经济机制。我们认为，该文更令人信服地记录了过度反应，而非将代表性孤立为 underlying mechanism。我们重新审视了银行信息环境的作用、数据生成过程、COVID时期的不确定性、内生性银行反应、监管影响，以及CECL（当前预期信用损失）结果相对于IFRS 9采用者子公司的解释。尽管若干额外分析支持有偏预期，但另一些分析则提示对机制的解读应更为谨慎。我们的总体看法是，若将证据更直接地围绕银行预期形成中的过度反应及其对拨备的含义来构建，同时为多种共存机制以及关于行为力量如何进入银行预测环境的未来研究留出更大空间，该文的核心贡献将得到加强。

after.abstract_zh: Bhojraj等（2026）提供了新颖的证据，表明系统重要性大型银行的内部贷款损失预测会系统性地对新信息过度反应，且这种过度反应对贷款损失拨备具有经济意义上的重要性。我们的讨论聚焦于这些证据是否识别出了代表性偏差，而非更广泛的行为、制度与经济机制。我们认为，该文更令人信服地记录了过度反应，而非将代表性孤立为 underlying mechanism。我们重新审视了银行信息环境的作用、数据生成过程、COVID时期的不确定性、内生性银行反应、监管影响，以及CECL（当前预期信用损失）结果相对于IFRS 9采用者子公司的解释。尽管若干额外分析支持有偏预期，但另一些分析则提示对机制的解读应更为谨慎。我们的总体看法是，若将证据更直接地围绕银行预期形成中的过度反应及其对拨备的含义来构建，同时为多种共存机制以及关于行为力量如何进入银行预测环境的未来研究留出更大空间，该文的核心贡献将得到加强。

source_records.title: The role of accounting in the informal economy
source_records.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

The role of accounting in the informal economy

Conference Manuscript
The role of accounting in the informal economy☆

•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.
•
Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. This unique setting allows us to observe accounting in its foundational role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance mechanism.5The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 examines when and why informal firms voluntarily keep systematic accounting records. Next, Section 3 explores how accounting quality relates to access to credit. Finally, Section 4 examines how accounting quality is associated with managerial decisions regarding microenterprise growth plans and productivity. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

before.abstract_zh: 我们利用来自危地马拉、洪都拉斯和萨尔瓦多1426家企业的全新调查数据，考察在非正规经济中经营的微型企业自愿采用会计系统的情况及其与获得信贷和业务增长之间的关联。尽管不存在监管强制要求，44%的非正规微型企业仍保留系统性财务记录，其中约四分之三使用笔记本，四分之一使用数字记录。会计质量与所有者的创业动机、财务投入和管理能力密切相关。依赖较大供应商、向客户提供分期信贷、开展营销促销或采用更正式组织结构的非正规企业，也更可能采用结构化记账系统，这凸显了会计作为管理工具的作用，而非作为合规职能或进入正规经济的前兆。保留将业务账户与个人账户分开的笔记本的非正规企业，显著更可能申请并获得银行贷款。我们对获得信贷的推断也适用于多米尼加共和国的微型企业。此外，会计质量似乎即使在非正规企业中也支持贷款人的尽职调查，尤其是当贷款人更为专业时。使用更广泛的信贷市场地位衡量指标，我们发现会计质量在各信贷层级之间单调上升。最后，我们发现拥有更高质量会计系统的企业家更可能规划业务扩张。通过阐明低执法环境下会计选择背后的动机，本研究加深了我们对会计在新兴市场早期业务发展中基础性作用的理解。

source_records.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. The role of accounting in the informal economy☆

•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.
•
Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.JEL classificationG21; M13; M4; O17KeywordsInformal economy; Developing economies; Microenterprises; Recordkeeping; Accounting quality; Financial inclusion; Access to creditIntroductionThis study examines the relationship between voluntary accounting practices and the informal economy in developing countries, where firms largely operate outside tax and business registrations, and beyond government enforcement (Ulyssea, 2020). We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. This unique setting allows us to observe accounting in its foundational role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance mechanism.5The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 examines when and why informal firms voluntarily keep systematic accounting records. Next, Section 3 explores how accounting quality relates to access to credit. Finally, Section 4 examines how accounting quality is associated with managerial decisions regarding microenterprise growth plans and productivity. Shroff (2017) further shows that firms’ information sets change when they adopt new GAAP requirements, with real effects on their investment decisions (see Ferracuti and Stubben, 2019).Whether these findings generalize to the rudimentaryConclusionThis study provides new evidence on the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises in the informal economy. proposed.abstract:
•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.

Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.

Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

fields.authors: Marcela Aguilar a, Gary Lind b, K. Ramesh c
fields.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

after.title_zh: 会计在非正规经济中的作用
after.abstract_zh: 我们利用来自危地马拉、洪都拉斯和萨尔瓦多1426家企业的全新调查数据，考察在非正规经济中经营的微型企业自愿采用会计系统的情况及其与获得信贷和业务增长之间的关联。尽管不存在监管强制要求，44%的非正规微型企业仍保留系统性财务记录，其中约四分之三使用笔记本，四分之一使用数字记录。会计质量与所有者的创业动机、财务投入和管理能力密切相关。依赖较大供应商、向客户提供分期信贷、开展营销促销或采用更正式组织结构的非正规企业，也更可能采用结构化记账系统，这凸显了会计作为管理工具的作用，而非作为合规职能或进入正规经济的前兆。保留将业务账户与个人账户分开的笔记本的非正规企业，显著更可能申请并获得银行贷款。我们对获得信贷的推断也适用于多米尼加共和国的微型企业。此外，会计质量似乎即使在非正规企业中也支持贷款人的尽职调查，尤其是当贷款人更为专业时。使用更广泛的信贷市场地位衡量指标，我们发现会计质量在各信贷层级之间单调上升。最后，我们发现拥有更高质量会计系统的企业家更可能规划业务扩张。通过阐明低执法环境下会计选择背后的动机，本研究加深了我们对会计在新兴市场早期业务发展中基础性作用的理解。

Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets

This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.
