Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. Formal tests confirm that the difference between the two treatments is significant, suggesting that adding methodological knowledge to the conceptual content is crucial for an effective intervention.Second, we examine whether our treatments mitigate the subsequent price reversal. Using the same DID framework, we find that treatment stocks indeed exhibit a smaller reversal than control stocks in both markets. For an average treatment stock, a one-standard-deviation increase in accruals improves the post-EA return by approximately 4.2% in China and 3.9% in the US relative to control stocks. As with the announcement-period results, this effect is concentrated in the group that received both conceptual and methodological knowledge: the negative relation between accruals and post-EA returns is essentially eliminated in this combined treatment group, whereas in the conceptual-only group the relation also improves but remains statistically insignificant. Together, the evidence indicates that the education treatment is effective in mitigating accrual mispricing and highlights the vital role of practical, methodological tools in this process.We obtain similar results when using unexpected discretionary accruals (see Balsam et al., 2002) and when using the comparison group as the benchmark in the DID analysis. A placebo test based on historical accruals yields no treatment effects, suggesting that our results are falsifiable. Additionally, we find that the treatment effects are more pronounced when the investors engage more with the educational materials (e.g., increased reading, comments, retweets, likes, and saves on our posts, as well as more clicks on the hyperlinks within the posts).Further analysis of the treatment effects indicates that these effects likely arise from addressing financial knowledge gaps among unsophisticated investors. First, the treatment effects are concentrated on stocks dominated by retail investors. Second, the education treatments reduce order imbalance (i.e., excessive purchases) for retail investors in stocks with high accruals on the EA day, but no similar pattern emerges for institutional investors. Third, the treatment effects are more pronounced in firms located in regions with low financial literacy.Lastly, we conduct tests to address alternative explanations. First, no education effect is found when comparing the control and comparison groups, negating the impact of treatment salience. Second, the education effect is evident only for positive accruals, aligning with our education's focus on high accrual implications and refuting the notion that our exercises merely amplify attention to accruals. Third, the education effect persists one year after the experiment, with no new messages posted, suggesting that our treatment effect is not fear-induced. Fourth, the effect remains pronounced in stocks with high trading turnover, implying a limited impact from the spillover effect due to common ownership between the treatment and control stocks. Finally, our results stay robust after accounting for the fixed effect of industry × EA months and excluding EAs during the pandemic peak, indicating minimal distortion from the COVID-19 outbreak.Our study makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on the effects of financial knowledge in financial markets. Existing studies mainly focus on the effects of financial knowledge on individuals’ financial decisions and behaviors (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to directly test the influence of financial knowledge on asset pricing.Second, our study extends research that examines financial anomalies and pricing efficiency. McLean and Pontiff (2016) posit that the academic discovery of financial anomalies can enhance market efficiency by enabling investors to pinpoint arbitrage opportunities. Our research underscores that not only is the discovery of such knowledge vital, but its dissemination and the education of investors regarding it are also crucial for improving market efficiency.Third, previous studies on accrual anomaly rest on explanations such as risk (Khan, 2008; Chichernea et al., 2015), transaction costs (Collins et al., 2003; Mashruwala et al., 2006), limited attention (Hirshleifer et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2016), and insufficient supplementary accounting information (Louis et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2016). We extend this body of literature by demonstrating a new explanation, namely investors’ limited understanding of accounting accruals. This perspective also sheds light on the understanding of other price anomalies.Lastly, our research carries policy implications. Individuals in many developed and developing countries have low levels of financial literacy (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Merkoulova and Veld, 2022). Although many financial education programs have been introduced worldwide to rectify this problem (Kaiser et al., 2022), their efficacy remains debatable (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Our findings underscore the potential of social media platforms as tools for investor education. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of integrating methodological applications with conceptual explanations in financial education. This insight holds considerable relevance for the design and execution of financial education programs.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literature“Financial knowledge,” or “financial literacy,” refers to people's ability to process economic information and make informed financial decisions (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). abstract.text: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. Formal tests confirm that the difference between the two treatments is significant, suggesting that adding methodological knowledge to the conceptual content is crucial for an effective intervention.Second, we examine whether our treatments mitigate the subsequent price reversal. Using the same DID framework, we find that treatment stocks indeed exhibit a smaller reversal than control stocks in both markets. For an average treatment stock, a one-standard-deviation increase in accruals improves the post-EA return by approximately 4.2% in China and 3.9% in the US relative to control stocks. As with the announcement-period results, this effect is concentrated in the group that received both conceptual and methodological knowledge: the negative relation between accruals and post-EA returns is essentially eliminated in this combined treatment group, whereas in the conceptual-only group the relation also improves but remains statistically insignificant. Together, the evidence indicates that the education treatment is effective in mitigating accrual mispricing and highlights the vital role of practical, methodological tools in this process.We obtain similar results when using unexpected discretionary accruals (see Balsam et al., 2002) and when using the comparison group as the benchmark in the DID analysis. A placebo test based on historical accruals yields no treatment effects, suggesting that our results are falsifiable. Additionally, we find that the treatment effects are more pronounced when the investors engage more with the educational materials (e.g., increased reading, comments, retweets, likes, and saves on our posts, as well as more clicks on the hyperlinks within the posts).Further analysis of the treatment effects indicates that these effects likely arise from addressing financial knowledge gaps among unsophisticated investors. First, the treatment effects are concentrated on stocks dominated by retail investors. Second, the education treatments reduce order imbalance (i.e., excessive purchases) for retail investors in stocks with high accruals on the EA day, but no similar pattern emerges for institutional investors. Third, the treatment effects are more pronounced in firms located in regions with low financial literacy.Lastly, we conduct tests to address alternative explanations. First, no education effect is found when comparing the control and comparison groups, negating the impact of treatment salience. Second, the education effect is evident only for positive accruals, aligning with our education's focus on high accrual implications and refuting the notion that our exercises merely amplify attention to accruals. Third, the education effect persists one year after the experiment, with no new messages posted, suggesting that our treatment effect is not fear-induced. Fourth, the effect remains pronounced in stocks with high trading turnover, implying a limited impact from the spillover effect due to common ownership between the treatment and control stocks. Finally, our results stay robust after accounting for the fixed effect of industry × EA months and excluding EAs during the pandemic peak, indicating minimal distortion from the COVID-19 outbreak.Our study makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on the effects of financial knowledge in financial markets. Existing studies mainly focus on the effects of financial knowledge on individuals’ financial decisions and behaviors (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to directly test the influence of financial knowledge on asset pricing.Second, our study extends research that examines financial anomalies and pricing efficiency. McLean and Pontiff (2016) posit that the academic discovery of financial anomalies can enhance market efficiency by enabling investors to pinpoint arbitrage opportunities. Our research underscores that not only is the discovery of such knowledge vital, but its dissemination and the education of investors regarding it are also crucial for improving market efficiency.Third, previous studies on accrual anomaly rest on explanations such as risk (Khan, 2008; Chichernea et al., 2015), transaction costs (Collins et al., 2003; Mashruwala et al., 2006), limited attention (Hirshleifer et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2016), and insufficient supplementary accounting information (Louis et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2016). We extend this body of literature by demonstrating a new explanation, namely investors’ limited understanding of accounting accruals. This perspective also sheds light on the understanding of other price anomalies.Lastly, our research carries policy implications. Individuals in many developed and developing countries have low levels of financial literacy (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Merkoulova and Veld, 2022). Although many financial education programs have been introduced worldwide to rectify this problem (Kaiser et al., 2022), their efficacy remains debatable (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Our findings underscore the potential of social media platforms as tools for investor education. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of integrating methodological applications with conceptual explanations in financial education. This insight holds considerable relevance for the design and execution of financial education programs.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literature“Financial knowledge,” or “financial literacy,” refers to people's ability to process economic information and make informed financial decisions (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

after.title_zh: 知识就是力量：一项在中国和美国股票市场进行的实地实验
after.abstract_zh: 本研究考察金融知识对股票定价效率的因果效应。借助专门设计的投资者教育网站，我们开展了一项实地实验，在社交媒体上与中国和美国的投资者分享关于会计应计项目定价的见解。我们发现，相对于控制组股票，处理组股票的应计错误定价有所减少。当增强对应计项目概念性理解的知识与有助于应计项目定量应用的知识相结合时，这一效应尤为显著。此外，在投资者对教育内容参与更深但金融素养较低的股票中，处理效应更强。
